title: [Refactor] moe: Derive layer contracts from the selected quant method
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #44994
* __->__ #44993
* #44991
* #44480

## Motivation

A MoE quantization method can execute on Triton while the requested backend remains FlashInfer or AITER. Dispatch, weight preparation and routing must follow the layer that actually executes. Backend identity also does not prove that a native router implements the model's routing policy: AUTO-resolved NVFP4 must preserve custom routing and renormalization.

## Modifications

- Quantization methods expose their effective execution backend, including wrapped methods, secondary runners and direct kernels. FusedMoE binds dispatch, expert-ID layout, transport payloads, post-load transforms and each model router to that contract.
- TRT-LLM in-kernel routing requires a declared policy matching the model's scoring, grouping, bias, renormalization, custom-router and shared-slot behavior. Other routers retain materialized STANDARD output. Explicit `Default` enum value 0 remains a real policy, distinct from an unspecified selector.
- TRT-LLM routed adapters consume materialized weights without renormalizing them again. Unsupported materialized per-tensor FP8 input fails before the kernel; an undeclared per-tensor router retains the Triton fallback and its compatible weight layout.
- Materialized TRT-LLM routes include the routed factor for every effective quantization method, including compressed-tensors FP8/NVFP4 schemes. Grouped/biased fallback producers apply the factor independently of renormalization while preserving shared contributions. Native routers still apply their own factor once. Ordinary loaders zero untouched padded weight tails, including repeated loads.
- Preserve model-wide DP layout for fallback payloads, gate AITER-specific transforms on the effective backend, and keep weight-only helpers with no runner valid. Binding is idempotent for the same contract and rejects conflicting reuse. The gfx1250 W4A8 internal router rejects unsupported expert sharding.

Equivalent native policies are declared for normalized MiMoV2 grouped sigmoid/bias, BailingMoE grouped sigmoid/bias or plain softmax, and Cohere2 sigmoid. Other configurations remain materialized. DeepSeek's logits-only dual-stream graph requires a BYPASSED router even when this PR is used independently.

Llama4 FP8 explicitly selects the model's top-1 sigmoid native policy. Gemma4 NVFP4 materializes its model router so selected-expert softmax weights retain the learned per-expert multiplier. These change behavior relative to the earlier native defaults; CPU contract tests cover the boundaries, but no full-model accuracy A/B is claimed for either model.

BailingLinear resolves its optional AWQ provider only when AWQ weights are loaded, so ordinary model construction does not require `vllm`. The Kimi constructor fixture declares the routing selector explicitly.

Requested-backend reads remain where they select a method, allocate compatible shapes or establish model-wide policy.

## CI fixture repair

Current head: `4275a5026050615139c3658a72b6a7d05d65b17f`.

The DeepSeek dual-stream test fixture now declares its native runner, BYPASSED TopK format and static expert dispatch policy. The production routing guard remains intact. This repairs the missing `topk` error in the registered CUDA graph test.

Validation: the original fixture reproduced the reported error at both the lower and upper PR production revisions. The corrected full test passed on one H200 GPU at both revisions, including opcheck, fullgraph compilation and CUDA graph capture/replay for replicated and non-replicated shared outputs. The tested fixture bytes match this commit. Applicable pre-commit checks passed.

GPU environment: Python 3.12.3, Torch 2.13.0+cu130, Triton 3.7.1, sgl-kernel 0.4.7 and FlashInfer 0.6.18. The test substitutes small CUDA operations for expert kernels; model loading, MoE numerical accuracy and full CI were not rerun for this fixture repair. Earlier validation below remains tied to its stated revisions.

## Earlier validation after rebase

Head: `fc2dd3d90bf86fe1b61741c1bb8d28a4e121dc8a`. Rebased onto main `553836c1647b3bfbeb266b49d76ec2c9df012425`; base `cheng/hot-fix/server-args-positional-api` is `77300dcce02c0b20d68cbc687bb56b54c4a97ace`.

- At this exact head, 6 focused CPU module(s) passed: 53 tests plus 85 reported subtests. Across all four PR heads, 15 focused modules completed 482 test executions plus 347 reported subtests, all passing.
- Each PR's full incremental tree matches the pre-rebase change applied to its rewritten base, retaining prior merge-only integration fixes. The stack remains #44480 -> #44991 -> #44993 -> #44994.
- Configured pre-commit checks passed over all 152 changed files in the full stack. Strict registration/entrypoint checks passed: 2,478 files / 3,012 registrations. CPU tests used Python 3.12.15 and Torch 2.14.1+cu130 with GPUs hidden.

GPU, full-model accuracy/throughput and full CI were not rerun for this rebase. Prior hardware measurements below remain evidence for their named earlier revisions; checked CUTLASS/Marlin/GGUF consumer sources are unchanged, which is source evidence rather than a new GPU run.

## Previous validation (before rebase)

Previous head: `b37b73a1ae1bdf3d73b6108deb76a14679a079b4`, based on #44991 and main `693d33330647c57f82e09ac39a34122fa46b5763`.

- At this exact head, 4 focused CPU modules passed: 28 tests plus 48 reported subtests, covering model policy constructors, shared scaling, ModelOpt dispatch and FP8 ownership. The full StandardDispatcher module also passed 21 tests plus 45 subtests on source bytes verified against this commit.
- The same new tests fail against the previous production sources for the intended missing scale, non-normalized shared compensation, model admission and dual-stream conditions. Compressed FP8/NVFP4 cases use real scheme/FusedMoE construction, TopK and dispatch with unit/nonunit factors and both renormalization choices. Model policy tests control FP8 quantization/native-provider boundaries; these CPU checks do not execute native quantized GEMMs.
- The integrated #44994 head separately passed 119 CPU tests across 12 modules, plus 200 reported subtests. Configured hooks and registration/entrypoint lint pass; strict parsing collects 2,472 files / 3,006 registrations. CPU execution: Python 3.12.15, Torch 2.14.1+cu130, GPUs hidden.

Earlier validation remains historical: the previous stack passed 856 CPU tests across 43 modules with 7 skips. At `97c954fdf334055dee221483622a5b8ae02c6e05`, a mixed block-FP8/BF16 Qwen3MoE smoke on 4 NVIDIA B300 GPUs (TP4/EP4) matched all 24 greedy IDs against Triton, with maximum generated-token logprob difference 0.0039258003. Neither result is full-model accuracy validation of this head.

Native TRT-LLM selector parity and full-model accuracy/performance have not been run for these policy changes. Unsupported ModelOpt per-tensor FP8 and compressed MXINT4 materialized-routing capabilities remain limited; rejection still occurs at apply rather than binding, and no compatibility claim is made for unverified conditional checkpoints. ROCm/NPU/XPU/gfx1250 execution and full CI remain unverified. Refs #44291, #40623; related #41636.

Motivation
DeepSeek-V4.1 verification rows from the same request score the same FP4 index-K cache. The existing Triton path decodes K independently for each query row; capacity-sized CUDA Graphs also leave substantial work on invisible positions.
This PR adds an opt-in SM90 grouped indexer that converts packed E2M1 to E5M2 in shared memory and uses FP8 WGMMA, reusing each decoded K tile across query rows. Hopper has no native MXFP4 MMA. The grouped path preserves the existing BF16 rounding points, ReLU, head weighting, and reduction order.
Changes
Optimize scale decoding in the existing SM90 Triton fallback.
Add a grouped CUDA path for H64/D128 request-major verification rows, with one query per warpgroup and shared K tiles of 64 positions.
Retain up to six decoded Q rows across 2/4/8 K tiles, with shape-dependent dispatch.
Compute
group_max_len
on device, skip completely invisible chunks/tiles, and write
-inf
. Partial tiles avoid reading invalid
req_to_token
entries.
Add a persistent scheduler: parallel device-side length loading, visible-chunk prefixes, a bounded resident CTA grid, and chunk sizing based on actual visible work. Q remains resident across assigned chunks from the same group.
Add a three-stage pipeline:
cp.async
loads packed tile i+2 while CUDA cores decode tile i+1 and WGMMA consumes tile i. Unaligned cache addresses retain a scalar-load fallback.
Extend registered tests for invisible tiles, partial groups, and CUDA Graph replay after changing lengths.
Dispatch and compatibility

accepts:
Value
Behavior
"auto"
(default)
Shape-dependent rectangular grid with Q residency and visibility skipping
"persistent"
Schedule visible chunks on a resident grid
"pipeline"
Persistent scheduling plus asynchronous packed-load/software-decode/WGMMA overlap
The grouped path remains opt-in; it is not enabled globally.
auto
does not automatically select persistent/pipeline. Measurements below show that the best mode depends on shape and visibility.
Scheduler metadata is CTA-local shared memory, recomputed on every invocation and graph replay. There is no CPU length readback, global allocation/counter, or request-slot scratch. Persistent modes support up to 1024 request groups and six rows per group, falling back to the single-tile path for larger inputs. title: [Fix] [NPU] support dsa pcp v2 with interleave & zigzag
body:
## Summary

Adapt GLM-5.2 (GlmMoeDsa) DSA prefill context parallelism to the CP V2 strategy flow, mirroring the DSV4 CP V2 support merged in #39427. After CP V1 was deprecated upstream, the NPU DSA path still referenced removed V1 metadata fields and could no longer run with --enable-prefill-cp.

## Changes

- **ascend_backend.py**: add prepare_dsa_cp_metadata which builds per-token local metadata for the Ascend sparse kernels (q/kv lengths from sharded local positions, per-token block-table rows selected by local batch ids); rewrite do_cp_balance_attn to a single npu_sparse_flash_attention call on the strategy-sharded local Q (no V1 prev/next balance split).
- **dsa_npu_indexer.py**: read V2 local metadata instead of the removed V1 attn_cp_metadata fields (actual_seq_q_prev_tensor / kv_len_prev_tensor / ...); rewrite do_npu_cp_balance_indexer as a single npu_lightning_indexer call.
- **deepseek_v2.py**: prepare DSA CP metadata at the inner-model entry (the eager CP runner invokes DeepseekV2Model directly); restore rebuild_cp_kv_cache, gathering the rank-local latent KV into full sequence order via cp_gather_full_sequence_states.
- **forward_mha.py**: on NPU with CP active, gather kv_a/k_pe to full sequence order before writing, since out_cache_loc spans the full sequence under CP V2.
- **unit tests**: add `test/registered/unit/layers/cp/test_dsa_cp_metadata.py` covering the zigzag/interleave block layout, local row selection, padding alignment, the `is_cp_active` gate, and the GLM DSA layer-split helpers.

The first commit fixes the attn_cp_tp_broadcast_pyobj broadcast order for attn-CP > 1 (broadcast along the attn-TP 0 line first, then TP).

## Testing

Full-model verification on a 4-node Ascend 910B3 cluster (32 NPUs/node) with GLM-5.2-w8a8 (GlmMoeDsa) in PD disaggregation:

- **Prefill** (2 nodes, 209/212): `--tp-size 8 --pp-size 4 --attn-cp-size 8 --enable-prefill-cp --cp-strategy interleave --chunked-prefill-size 8192 --max-prefill-tokens 65536 --mem-fraction-static 0.88`, NEXTN spec (num-steps 1, draft 2)
- **Decode** (2 nodes, 216/217): `--tp-size 32 --dp-size 32 --ep-size 32`, NEXTN spec (num-steps 3, draft 4)
- Key envs: `DEEPEP_HCCL_BUFFSIZE=2048`, `SGLANG_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=18,20,24,16`, `SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_ALL_CP_RANKS_TRANSFER=1`, `SGLANG_ENABLE_SPEC_V2=1`, `MALLOC_CHECK_=3`
- Client: vllm bench serve through the sglang PD router (16 prompts, concurrency 4, input 65536 / output 2500)

### Throughput / latency results

| config | result | TTFT mean / median / P99 | TPOT | throughput |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| zigzag + chunk 4096 | :white_check_mark: 16/16 | 9.45s / 5.85s / 26.05s | 26.89 ms | 3370 tok/s |
| interleave + chunk 8192 (fixed len) | :white_check_mark: 16/16 | 9.12s / 6.08s / 20.05s | 25.70 ms | 3570 tok/s |
| interleave + chunk 8192 (variable input 40960–90112) | :white_check_mark: 16/16 | 7.82s / 6.94s / 15.53s | 25.85 ms | 3550 tok/s |

The zigzag + chunk 8192 crash is a deep_ep CAM dispatch buffer overflow (`HCCL_BUFFSIZE is too SMALL`, 3304MB needed > 2048MB) triggered when a pass dispatches the whole 8076-token batch per rank; chunk 4096 caps the per-rank dispatch at ~1.78GB. Interleave keeps CP active on every pass (1024 tokens/rank, ~604MB), so it is safe with chunk 8192.

## Performance: single-call vs two-call DSA attention (zigzag)

Measured on the 4-node 2p2d GLM-5.2-w8a8 stack (b072 image; 2 prefill nodes tp8 x cp8 x pp4 zigzag + 2 decode nodes tp32 x dp32, NEXTN 1x2/3x4), fixed-length 64k-input x 8-concurrent requests:

| variant | success | wall | TTFT mean (min/max) | e2e mean (min/max) | decode tok/s |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| single fused call (shipped) | 8/8 | 38.13s | 21.70s (8.72 / 33.32) | 26.05s (12.96 / 38.12) | 53.7 |
| two calls, per-sequence metadata (experiment) | 8/8 | 38.21s | 21.79s (8.81 / 33.43) | 26.10s (12.95 / 38.20) | 53.6 |

The two-call variant splits the local Q into prev/next halves and issues two `npu_sparse_flash_attention` calls with per-sequence metadata. It was built as an experiment during development; after fixing a batch-local `actual_seq_lengths_query` restart for the second call (plus empty-shard / block-table-row / contiguous-view guards), its output matches the single-call path exactly (max element diff 0.0, verified with an in-model probe at 64k). End-to-end performance is identical (<0.5% difference), so this PR ships the single-call implementation for simplicity.

Accuracy spot-check on the two-call variant (full 68-layer model): "What is 6 times 7?" -> "42", "What is 7 times 8?" -> "56".

title: github:vllm-project/FlashMLA:26 fetched implementation patch
VibeTensor: System Software for Deep Learning, Fully Generated by AI Agents
body: VIBETENSOR is an open-source research system software stack for deep learning, generated by LLM-powered coding agents under high-level human guidance. In this paper, "fully generated" refers to code provenance: implementation changes were produced and applied as agent-proposed diffs; validation relied on agent-run builds, tests, and differential checks, without per-change manual diff review. It implements a PyTorch-style eager tensor library with a C++20 core (CPU+CUDA), a torch-like Python overlay via nanobind, and an experimental Node.js/TypeScript interface. Unlike thin bindings, VIBETENSOR includes its own tensor/storage system, schema-lite dispatcher, reverse-mode autograd, CUDA runtime (streams/events/graphs), a stream-ordered caching allocator with diagnostics, and a stable C ABI for dynamically loaded operator plugins. We view this release as a milestone for AI-assisted software engineering: it shows coding agents can generate a coherent deep learning runtime spanning language bindings down to CUDA memory management, validated primarily by builds and tests. We describe the architecture, summarize the workflow used to produce and validate the system, and evaluate the artifact. We report repository scale and test-suite composition, and summarize reproducible microbenchmarks from an accompanying AI-generated kernel suite, including fused attention versus PyTorch SDPA/FlashAttention. We also report end-to-end training sanity checks on 3 small workloads (sequence reversal, ViT, miniGPT) on NVIDIA H100 (Hopper, SM90) and Blackwell-class GPUs; multi-GPU results are Blackwell-only and use an optional CUTLASS-based ring-allreduce plugin gated on CUDA 13+ and sm103a toolchain support. Finally, we discuss failure modes in generated system software, including a "Frankenstein" composition effect where locally correct subsystems interact to yield globally suboptimal performance.

title: TPI-LLM: Serving 70B-scale LLMs Efficiently on Low-resource Edge Devices
body:
Large model inference is shifting from cloud to edge due to concerns about
the privacy of user interaction data. However, edge devices often struggle with
limited computing power, memory, and bandwidth, requiring collaboration across
multiple devices to run and speed up LLM inference. Pipeline parallelism, the
mainstream solution, is inefficient for single-user scenarios, while tensor
parallelism struggles with frequent communications. In this paper, we argue
that tensor parallelism can be more effective than pipeline on low-resource
devices, and present a compute- and memory-efficient tensor parallel inference
system, named TPI-LLM, to serve 70B-scale models. TPI-LLM keeps sensitive raw
data local in the users' devices and introduces a sliding window memory
scheduler to dynamically manage layer weights during inference, with disk I/O
latency overlapped with the computation and communication. This allows larger
models to run smoothly on memory-limited devices. We analyze the communication
bottleneck and find that link latency, not bandwidth, emerges as the main
issue, so a star-based allreduce algorithm is implemented. Through extensive
experiments on both emulated and real testbeds, TPI-LLM demonstrated over 80%
less time-to-first-token and token latency compared to Accelerate, and over 90%
compared to Transformers and Galaxy, while cutting the peak memory footprint of
Llama 2-70B by 90%, requiring only 3.1 GB of memory for 70B-scale models.

title:
EN-T: Optimizing Tensor Computing Engines Performance via Encoder-Based
  Methodology
body:
Tensor computations, with matrix multiplication being the primary operation,
serve as the fundamental basis for data analysis, physics, machine learning,
and deep learning. As the scale and complexity of data continue to grow
rapidly, the demand for tensor computations has also increased significantly.
To meet this demand, several research institutions have started developing
dedicated hardware for tensor computations. To further improve the
computational performance of tensor process units, we have reexamined the issue
of computation reuse that was previously overlooked in existing architectures.
As a result, we propose a novel EN-T architecture that can reduce chip area and
power consumption. Furthermore, our method is compatible with existing tensor
processing units. We evaluated our method on prevalent microarchitectures, the
results demonstrate an average improvement in area efficiency of 8.7\%, 12.2\%,
and 11.0\% for tensor computing units at computational scales of 256 GOPS, 1
TOPS, and 4 TOPS, respectively. Similarly, there were energy efficiency
enhancements of 13.0\%, 17.5\%, and 15.5\%.

title: Canzona: A Unified, Asynchronous, and Load-Balanced Framework for Distributed Matrix-based Optimizers
body: The scaling of Large Language Models (LLMs) drives interest in matrix-based optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, Muon, SOAP) for their convergence efficiency; yet their requirement for holistic updates conflicts with the tensor fragmentation in distributed frameworks like Megatron. Existing solutions are suboptimal: synchronous approaches suffer from computational redundancy, while layer-wise partitioning fails to reconcile this conflict without violating the geometric constraints of efficient communication primitives. To bridge this gap, we propose Canzona, a Unified, Asynchronous, and Load-Balanced framework that decouples logical optimizer assignment from physical parameter distribution. For Data Parallelism, we introduce an alpha-Balanced Static Partitioning strategy that respects atomicity while neutralizing the load imbalance. For Tensor Parallelism, we design an Asynchronous Compute pipeline utilizing Micro-Group Scheduling to batch fragmented updates and hide reconstruction overhead. Extensive evaluations on the Qwen3 model family (up to 32B parameters) on 256 GPUs demonstrate that our approach preserves the efficiency of established parallel architectures, achieving a 1.57x speedup in end-to-end iteration time and reducing optimizer step latency by 5.8x compared to the baseline.

title: feat(agentx): run AgentX on upstream AIPerf / feat(agentx): 在上游 AIPerf 上运行 AgentX
body:
## Summary

AgentX currently runs on `agentx-harness==1.0.12`, SemiAnalysis's fork of AIPerf. Upstream `ai-dynamo/aiperf` now contains everything AgentX relies on: the fork was ported in ai-dynamo/aiperf#1413, and the SPAWN fixes landed as #1540 (roll back delayed SPAWN children at the sending cutoff) and #1567 (pin SPAWN children under their own sticky entry). This PR moves AgentX to upstream AIPerf at `8aa7039f872cd029f05a4c313fb8759e9a482cd3`, removing the fork from the benchmark path.

- `infx/bench/agentic/requirements.txt` installs AIPerf from the pinned commit's source tarball, so the serving containers don't need git.
- The replay runs `aiperf profile --scenario inferencex-agentx-mvp`. Recipe and workflow values still win.
- `job_event.json` records the pinned commit as `versions.aiperf_sha`. `agentx_harness` stays in the schema for older records and is null for new ones.
- The standalone guide and READMEs now describe `aiperf profile`.

**Behavior changes vs 1.0.12 (why this is a perf-changelog entry for every agentic config):**
- A SPAWN subagent's first turn keeps the parent's messages (ai-dynamo/aiperf#1555). This changes the request content and ISL of those turns.
- Every request also carries `X-Session-Affinity` with the correlation ID (upstream default `AIPERF_HTTP_X_SESSION_AFFINITY_FROM_CORRELATION_ID=true`).
- A stall watchdog no longer cancels streaming requests (#1568), and a stalled benchmark fails instead of waiting indefinitely (#1501).

Apart from these, the benchmark config AIPerf builds is unchanged. For the default, FAST, under-900 s and all-opt-ins points, the CLI parse, plan build and scenario check on the installed pin give the same values as 1.0.12 for all shared settings, except the scenario name (`agentx` → `inferencex-agentx-mvp`).

**Open issues (draft):**
- **Pre-existing, not fixed here:** for `dynamo-*` frameworks with conversation-aware routing, `replay.py` passes `--use-dynamo-conv-aware-routing` and `--dynamo-session-timeout-seconds`. Neither 1.0.12 nor upstream AIPerf accepts these flags ("Unknown option"), so those points fail on `main` today, and this PR keeps the same flags.
- `validate_perf_changelog` rejects the `"*"` entry because matrix planning fails on `benchmarks/single_node/srt-slurm-recipes/qwen3.5/sglang/h100-fp8/agentic.yaml` (KV offloading / DRAM override mismatch). This PR does not touch that config.
- No GPU runs yet. The `"*"` entry sweeps every agentic config, so the sweep scope needs agreeing before a primary sweep label is applied.
- Overlaps #4288, which passes `AIPERF_SLICE_DURATION`; this PR fixes `--slice-duration 1.0`.

title: [NVIDIA][AgentX] GB300 GLM-5.2 NVFP4 Dynamo+SGLang: PP4-prefill disagg and TP4/TP8 agg points / GB300 GLM-5.2 NVFP4 Dynamo+SGLang：PP4 prefill 分离式与 TP4/TP8 聚合配置点
body:
Moves both GB300 GLM-5.2 NVFP4 Dynamo + SGLang AgentX keys to `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-20261016-a93f16f0` (multi-arch digest pinned). The aggregated key runs the ai-dynamo `1.6.0.dev20261015` bundled in the image (`dynamo.install: false`). The disaggregated key installs the ai-dynamo `1.6.0.dev20261016` wheel. The disaggregated points move to one PP4 prefill worker per node (sgl-project/sglang#39378).

| Config key | Topology | Conc | Nodes | Key settings |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `glm5.2-fp4-gb300-dynamo-sglang-agentic-agg` | TP4 | 1 | 1 | MTP 4 steps, fp8 KV cache, cutedsl BF16 GEMM, 8 running requests and decode graphs, HiCache 100 GB/rank |
| | TP8 | 1 | 2 | MTP 5 steps, 2 running requests and decode graphs, HiCache 100 GB/rank |
| `glm5.2-fp4-gb300-dynamo-sglang-agentic-disagg` | 1x PP4 prefill + 5x TP4 decode | 30 | 6 | prefill HiCache 100 GB/rank, decode radix cache, 24 requests per decode worker |
| | 1x PP4 prefill + 3x TP4 decode | 40 | 4 | as c30 |
| | 1x PP4 prefill + 1x DEP8 decode | 56 | 3 | 8k prefill chunks, prefill mem-fraction 0.75, 32 requests per decode rank |
| | 3x PP4 prefill + 1x DEP8 decode | 216 | 5 | prefill layer split 20,20,20,18, 32 requests per decode rank |
| | 3x PP4 prefill + 1x DEP8 decode | 264 | 5 | as c216 with 8k prefill chunks, prefill mem-fraction 0.88, HiCache 185 GB/rank, decode mem-fraction 0.94 |
| | 4x PP4 prefill + 1x DEP16 decode | 256 | 8 | 32 requests per decode rank |

- Every point uses EAGLE MTP on the checkpoint's built-in NextN head with HiCache write_back DRAM KV offload. Prefill and decode use the same MTP settings (5 steps, top-k 1, 6 draft tokens; TP4 agg uses 4 steps and 5 draft tokens).
- Synthetic acceptance follows the golden GLM-5.2 thinking-on AL: 3.33 at 4 MTP steps and 3.61 at 5. No recipe sets `SGLANG_SIMULATE_ACC_*` or `SGLANG_NVFP4_CKPT_FP8_NEXTN_MOE`.
- KV transfer uses NIXL; no recipe sets `UCX_*` variables. DEP decode workers set `expert-parallel-size` explicitly to match the master config's `ep`.
- Prefill workers advertise a 3600 s session-affinity TTL to the prefill router; decode workers advertise an active-request weight of 8192 to the decode router, so decode routing balances request counts.
- `dram-utilization` is raised to 0.85 for the disaggregated key so c264's 185 GB/rank prefill HiCache plus the DSA-indexer host pool fit; the aggregated key stays at 0.80.
- Tachometer and the Dynamo OTel collector are disabled.
- Removes the aggregated TP8 c2/c4 points, the DEP4-prefill 1P2D/1P4D/1P6D points, the DEP8/DEP16 2P1D c192 point, and `disagg-2p1d-p-dep8-d-dep16-c192-mtp.yaml`, which only that point used.

- `glm5.2-fp4-gb300-dynamo-sglang-agentic-agg`：
  - TP4 c1（1 个节点）：MTP 4 步，fp8 KV cache，cutedsl BF16 GEMM，8 个运行请求与 decode graph，HiCache 每 rank 100 GB。
  - TP8 c1（2 个节点）：MTP 5 步，2 个运行请求与 decode graph，HiCache 每 rank 100 GB。
- `glm5.2-fp4-gb300-dynamo-sglang-agentic-disagg`：

  - 1P1D c56（1 个 PP4 prefill + 1 个 DEP8 decode，3 个节点）：prefill chunk 8k，prefill mem-fraction 0.75。
  - 3P1D c216（3 个 PP4 prefill + 1 个 DEP8 decode，5 个节点）：prefill 层划分 20,20,20,18。
  - 3P1D c264（5 个节点）：同 c216，另使用 8k prefill chunk、prefill mem-fraction 0.88、HiCache 每 rank 185 GB、decode mem-fraction 0.94。
  - 4P1D c256（4 个 PP4 prefill + 1 个 DEP16 decode，8 个节点）。
  - DEP decode 每个 rank 32 个请求。
- 所有配置点均使用基于 checkpoint 内置 NextN head 的 EAGLE MTP，并启用 HiCache write_back DRAM KV offload。prefill 与 decode 使用相同的 MTP 设置（5 步、top-k 1、6 个 draft token；TP4 聚合为 4 步、5 个 draft token）。

- KV 传输使用 NIXL，recipe 中未设置任何 `UCX_*` 变量。DEP decode worker 显式设置 `expert-parallel-size`，与 master config 的 `ep` 一致。

- 关闭 Tachometer 与 Dynamo OTel collector。
- 移除聚合 TP8 c2/c4、DEP4 prefill 的 1P2D/1P4D/1P6D、DEP8/DEP16 2P1D c192 配置点，以及仅被 2P1D 使用的 `disagg-2p1d-p-dep8-d-dep16-c192-mtp.yaml`。

title: [RFC] Benchmark valid-prefix sorting and count prefetch for compact dispatch
body:
Add a standalone experimental benchmark that separates valid-prefix deterministic sorting from early receive-count copies for compact BF16 dispatch. It compares four factorial arms with both native sync-free and native deferred materialization, using the same independent GEMM work and synchronized end-to-end readiness timing.

This is a **draft experiment/benchmark PR**, with no production API or default change. On eight H200 GPUs, all eight measured scenarios remain slower than native deferred. Valid-prefix sorting helps relative to the matching full-capacity sort, while early count copies do not provide a consistent additional benefit. The documentation retains all six arms, all cases and all three fresh-process summaries.

The existing GPU study covers 1920 correctness/smoke rank/cases plus 1152 full-performance preflight rank/cases: independent dispatch-reference equality, counts, combine, cached replay, saved-view backward, both allocation streams, both record-stream policies, and uneven/duplicate/skewed/masked routes. The published execution code matches the measured script; only its docstring and historical-source log label changed. Local compilation, AST equivalence, evidence-count checks and `git diff --check` passed before publication.

See `tests/ep/prefix_sort_experiment.md` for reproduction, complete results and scope. This is a one-NVLink-domain compact BF16 experiment; it does not establish full-training gains or cover FP8/expanded/hybrid dispatch.

Co-authored with
@iclementine
(the first SM90 ring buffer) and
@Hyaloid
(cluster and multicast).
This adds a single-kernel SM90 FP8 MegaMoE next to the two-kernel path from
#383
. One task stream runs both GEMMs with L2 trailing L1 by a fixed lag, and the L1 activation pool becomes a ring sized around that lag instead of the token bound. On 8×H100 EP8 that is
1.44–1.56× at 2048 tokens/rank and 1.33–1.43× at 8192
against the summed device time of
#383
's two kernels, on 4.3–4.6× less symmetric memory. It is opt-in and additive.
Performance
One 8×H100 node, EP8, this repo's own harness as this PR leaves it. Both arms size the symmetric buffer from the harness's default 8192-token bound rather than from the batch, so every row of a table runs on the same buffer: 3023 → 700 MiB on flash and 5083 → 1113 MiB on pro.

tests/bench_mega_moe_sm90.py
are covered: fused/split is 0.642–0.977 over 64–8192 tokens/rank.
pro at 1024 sits between the two regimes. Each rank streams 3.2 GB of expert weights per call on that shape against 0.8 GB on flash, and at 128 tokens per expert both arms are still within 1.5–1.7× of the HBM floor for those bytes, so there is little exposed L1 → L2 serialisation left for the fusion to hide; flash at 1024 runs 192 tokens per expert and its split arm is 3× its floor. These are the two size queries the buffers call, which is also where the harness reads the 8192 figures. Below the 1024-token lag threshold the fused buffer keeps the full pool and saves 7–20 %; from 1024 the ring takes over, and the saving grows with the bound because only the L1/L2 activation pools come from the ring while the dispatch inputs and the combine buffer still scale with it.
Benchmark method, the noisy cell, and a third shape
8×H100 80 GB HBM3, EP8, driver 535.230.02, CUDA 13.3 (V13.3.73), PyTorch 2.13.0a0. One node, all eight GPUs held for the whole run with no other compute process on them. This repo's own harness, as this PR leaves it:
python tests/bench_mega_moe_sm90.py --model-config {flash,pro} --batches <M> \
    --num-max-tokens-per-rank 8192 --arms split fused --num-processes 8
Each number is
bench_kineto
device time summed over that arm's kernels (
sm90_fp8_mega_moe_l1_impl
+
sm90_fp8_mega_moe_l2_impl
for split,
sm90_fp8_fused_mega_moe_impl
for fused), with the harness's 8 GB L2 flush, ~10 ms sleep and
dist.barrier
before each call — a burst duty cycle, not a steady state. 20 calls per observation, the harness's own three observations per round above 128 tokens/rank and 50 at or below it, max over the eight ranks, then median over observations. Three rounds with the arms bracketed —
split fused
, then
fused split
, then
split fused
— so each cell is the median of three round medians, and the band in parentheses is the smallest and largest of the three per-round ratios. Lag units, the ring they size, and the single-wave order are defined under How it works.
The fused arm passes
num_tokens_bound=M
on every call, which is what a caller whose ranks all run the same count would pass; the split path has no such argument and needs none, since none of its heuristics key on a rank-uniform count. That keyword is what makes the 64 / 128 / 256 rows take the single-wave order here, and on flash it also runs the 512 to 4096 rows at a 14-unit lag instead of the 29 its ring is sized for (
DG_PRINT_CONFIGS
reports
l2_lag_units
4014 against 4029); pro's buffer lag is 22 at this capacity and its bounded calls keep it.
The one cell where the fused arm is the noisier of the two is flash at 256 tokens/rank, 12 % from a single high round against the split arm's 5.6 % — that row's band (0.868–1.029) is spread and not a stable difference, and no other cell's fused spread is above 4 %.
Every cell runs the default intermediate-scale granularity, 128 on both of these shapes. The fused arm asks for PDL at ≤ 256 tokens/rank while
#383
's kernels carry no griddepcontrol at all, so on the 64 / 128 / 256 rows the fused Kineto duration contains its own
griddepcontrol.wait
— part of why those rows show the smallest margins.
A third shape — 4096 / 2048 with 288 experts and top-8, i.e. 36 experts per rank instead of 32 or 48 — was taken once rather than in rounds, at the same 8192-token bound: fused/split is 0.950, 0.968, 0.955, 0.739, 0.613, 0.607, 0.634 and 0.677 at 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096 and 8192 tokens per rank, and the symmetric buffer goes from 4000 to 857 MiB. Read the first three rows as "no worse" given the drift above; the rest behaves like the flash table.
How it works
The kernel fixes the order first. The B loader enumerates a stream in which a token block's L2 tasks sit
lag
units after its L1 tasks, in groups of
group
units; a unit is up to 8 consecutive m-blocks of one expert. The host picks
lag = clamp(round(0.45 × units), 8, 64)
and
group = 4
, with
units
estimated from the call's token bound and the buffer capacity, not the routed count.
It also differs from
#383
numerically: one scale per 64 or 128 contiguous K elements of the intermediate activation (
l2_act_sf_gran_k
, a buffer parameter) where
#383
always writes one per 64, and the raw scale where
#383
's SM90 kernel rounds it to the next power of two. Both are inside the shared test's tolerance against the same reference.
Why the order and not the pool size, and the lag ladder
The split path materialises every rank's L1 output before L2 starts, so its pool is sized for all tokens of all ranks and the GEMMs never overlap. Fusing them buys the overlap and does not fix the pool, because nothing bounds how far L2 trails L1. Worse, L2's NVLink combine scatter starts while the dispatch pull is still running on the same per-rank egress. A ladder that pins the ring at 356 blocks and varies only the lag still leaves the short-lag calls the slow ones, so what costs is the order and not the pool size.
Event traces on an instrumented build of this kernel (8×H100, 8192 tokens/rank) put the end of the dispatch pull at 2671 µs from kernel start when the lag is 8 units and at 1102 µs when it is 40 — 2541 µs against 1044 µs measured from each run's own head barrier, which completes at 130 µs and at 58 µs. At the lag this picks, 55 % of the L1 tiles are done when the pull ends.
Ring sizing, recycling, and why that granularity
Fixing the order makes the ring size arithmetic: at most
8 × (lag + group)
blocks of L1 output are live, so the pool becomes a ring of
8 × (lag + group) + 4
slots, asserted against that live set on the host. L1 epilogues wait on
l2_empty
before overwriting a slot's previous generation, and dispatch warps publish any pending arrival before blocking, so no wait can point at unpublished work.
kSm90FusedLagRingMargin
is the
+ 4
. Recycling reuses the
l1/l2_full
counters and adds the matching
empty
counters plus launch-parity banks for the flags that would otherwise need all-rank head and exit barriers. A ring clamped to the full pool never wraps and is exempt from the host assertion. Consumers replay the tile table the B loader publishes — payload first, then an acquire-loaded tag — and the L2 tail after the last L1 task is handed out by an atomic ticket. Calls whose worst-case pool already fits, and buffers below the lag threshold, keep a single-wave order instead.
Also in the diff: arrival publishes batched up to 16 rows, on calls above a token threshold whose ring covers the batch; an early combine in which math warps reduce tokens whose selected experts have all published while the all-rank barrier is still pending; a BLOCK_M=64, 256-wide split-N tile with a sliced combine queue for decode-sized calls;
num_tokens_bound
; and an XOR bank swizzle on the L2 epilogue staging. The early combine stages whole rows in the pre-barrier shared memory where they fit and in chunks otherwise, and falls back from 2 chunks to 4 when 2 do not fit — which is what keeps 7168 hidden working at decode sizes, where the tile leaves that region smallest.
The scale width defaults to 128 when
hidden % 512 == 0
and
2 × intermediate_hidden % 512 == 0
(the condition for the 256-wide decode tile) and to 64 otherwise. 128 is the grouping the non-fused DeepEP + grouped-GEMM path uses for this activation; it halves the act-SF pool and lets each 128-K step of L2's mainloop take one scale group and one rescale instead of two.
#360
reports an end-to-end accuracy issue it suspects came from quantising this same activation per-64 where the rest of the stack does per-128.
The scale itself is
sf = max(amax, 1e-10) / 448
, the raw scale, which is also what the shared test's reference computes (with a 1e-4 floor on amax instead of 1e-10) and what the sgl-project SM90 kernel this data path comes from uses. The fused arm keeps the full FP8 range, the split one keeps an exactly representable scale.
What to check before merging
Two shared files are rewritten rather than added to, and they are the part of the diff to read hardest.
In
comm/barrier.cuh
(+50/−14) the two waits become generic over the workspace type and, under
BarrierTimeoutPolicy::TrapOnly
, call
handle_*_timeout
after leaving the wait loop rather than from inside it. The fused kernel needs that shape: a
trap;
inside the loop makes ptxas allocate that region's registers against the kernel's launch bound and ignore its
setmaxnreg.inc
, which spills.
csrc/jit/kernel_runtime.hpp
(+10/−5) is the other: a launcher can now force the PDL launch attribute instead of leaving it to the global flag, and no existing launcher passes the new argument.

#383

Diagnostic

TrapOnly

sm_90a

--register-usage-level=10

Diagnostic

For
#383

REG:168 STACK:0 SHARED:1024 LOCAL:0

REG:96 STACK:24 SHARED:1024 LOCAL:0

variants and the branch targets shifted around the deadline compare. Its own accuracy test passes unchanged (see Tests).
The PDL change only adds the launch attribute, never removes it, and it applies to a kernel compiled with griddepcontrol, which the fused path is and
#383
's kernels are not.
num_tokens_bound
needs a warning label.
It must be identical on every rank and cover every rank's own count, e.g. the max over ranks of the local batch. Each rank rejects a bound below its own count or above the buffer's capacity, but nothing compares the ranks, and a bound below a peer's count hangs: this rank's pool is then sized for fewer rows than will arrive, so the ring reuses a slot inside one wave.
None
means the buffer capacity, and a bound below it is what lets a large buffer take the single-wave order.
What a per-rank token count changes, and what it does not
The rules that key on a per-rank token count fall back to this rank's own count when the bound is omitted, so ranks with different local batches can pick different orders. Nothing cross-rank rides on that: the ring capacity is the buffer's, and the call's lag comes from the bound -- the capacity when none is given -- clamped to the buffer's, so both hold the same value on every rank.
One rule keys on the token count in a way worth spelling out.
block_m
is chosen from this rank's token count (
num_tokens * num_ranks * num_topk / num_experts >= 64
flips it 64 -> 128),
block_m
sets
num_stages
through the per-stage smem cost, and early combine turns on only when
hidden / block_k
and
intermediate_hidden / block_k
both exceed
num_stages
. So it is a function of the shapes only where the shape leaves margin, and passing
num_tokens_bound
does not make it uniform -- the tile choice reads the raw count. On the shapes here the margin is wide: 4096/2048 gives 16 k-blocks and 7168/3072 gives 24, against 3 stages at both M=2048 and M=8192, and the mode never flips. I had to take
intermediate_hidden
down to 640, which no shipped config uses, before the flip appeared -- 287 tokens gives 7 stages and mode 0, 288 gives 4 stages and mode 1. What does move per rank on production shapes is
block_m
,
block_n
and
num_stages
, and since those are JIT template arguments like the mode itself, ranks with different local batches compile and launch different instantiations of the same kernel. They still meet at the same pre-combine rendezvous: same signal word, same phase and sign rule, same expected arrival count, one signal per rank either way. If the modes ever did disagree the cost would be throughput, not liveness -- a rank on the early-combine path only early-combines tokens whose experts all live on ranks that took the same path, and the rest fall through to the ordinary combine after the barrier. One gap worth noting on its own: the early-combine copy of the barrier keeps the 60 s deadline on the cross-rank signal wait but not on its two grid syncs, which the shared
grid_sync
does guard.
The shape domain is a strict subset.
intermediate_hidden ≤ 4096
, rejected when the buffer is sized, where
#383
's split path accepts 4224. No shared-expert fusion either, same as
#383
's SM90 path.
No CI coverage.
Neither SM90 MegaMoE test runs in CI, since both need 8 GPUs and NVLink. Everything under Tests below was run by hand on one 8×H100 node, sm_90a, CUDA 13.3.
fused=True
at buffer allocation (
--arms fused
in the benchmark harness,
--fused
in the accuracy test) selects it;
#383
's kernel, heuristics and launcher are untouched, and its two Python entry points only gain keywords that default to today's behaviour. The two arms are separate buffers, JIT instantiations and host paths. The shape subset, the quantisation difference and the missing CI are why this is opt-in rather than the default. A default needs a fallback for the shapes it cannot serve, and flipping it would change existing callers' outputs bit for bit without them asking. Say so and I'll flip it: the rounding is one line, the fallback a shape check in the buffer query.

fp8_mega_moe

fused

Full API surface
Opting in costs one keyword at allocation and nothing per call:
fp8_mega_moe
dispatches on the buffer type.
get_symm_buffer_for_sm90_mega_moe(..., fused=False, num_experts_per_wave=None, l2_act_sf_gran_k=None)
and

num_experts_per_wave
:
None
= ring from the lag rule (full pool below the threshold),
-1
= ring sized for an automatically chosen expert wave,
N
= capacity for a wave of
min(N, E_local)
experts, never more than the full pool. It is how the ring test builds its auto-wave and full-pool arms.
l2_act_sf_gran_k

get_symm_buffer_size_for_sm90_fused_mega_moe

(bytes, slicer, num_ring_tokens, l2_lag_encoded)

The rules that fall back to this rank's own count when
num_tokens_bound
is omitted are whether the call takes the single-wave order instead of the lag order, the arrival-publish batch and its eager variant, and whether a decode-sized call takes PDL. The single-wave order additionally needs the worst-case pool at the call's bound -- the buffer's capacity when none is given -- to fit the ring.
Tests: the accuracy runs, the bound replay, and the eight ring shapes
tests/test_mega_moe_sm90.py --fused
runs the file's 39 scenarios at both scale granularities, minus the 4224
intermediate_hidden
one the fused path skips: 76 cases, all pass on 8 ranks, largest deviation 1e-4 against the 0.01 tolerance. The same file's split arm still passes unchanged on this branch: 39 scenarios, largest deviation 7e-4 against the same 0.01 tolerance.
tests/test_mega_moe_sm90_fused_ring.py
is new: it checks the lag ring
bitwise
against a full-pool control on eight shapes, four launches per buffer with skewed routing in between, exercising both launch-parity banks and the wrap. A fourth buffer replays those launches under each call's own
num_tokens_bound
, bit for bit again, then under a bound one alignment above capacity, which has to raise on the host before any rank launches. Sixteen cases pass, at most 1e-4 from the reference against the test's 0.07 tolerance.
The ring test takes ~2 min on 8 GPUs per granularity, and the sixteen cases are its eight shapes at both scale granularities. The shapes are the shared test's
hidden=1024
shape at 64, 256, 512, 1024 and 2048 tokens per rank, which straddles the 1024-token lag threshold from both sides; a 4096/2048/288/top-8 shape whose lag ring is 20992 of 135680 pool tokens, next to a 98304-token auto-wave ring; a 1024/1024/64/top-6 shape at a 5120-token capacity, 18944 ring tokens of a 246784-token pool next to an 81920-token auto-wave ring; and a 2-rank subgroup whose requested ring is larger than the pool and clamps to it. The verdict is all-reduced, so a single-rank mismatch reports instead of hanging.
The replay is where both things a bound can change get covered. The decode-sized launch is bounded at 256 tokens, so on the lag rings that one call runs the single-wave order against the same allocation running the lag order without a bound (
DG_PRINT_CONFIGS
reports
l2_lag_units
4008, 4014 or 4016 unbounded and 0 under the bound); and on the 5120-token shape the 3840-token launch runs an 11-unit lag under its own bound where the unbounded allocation runs the 14 its ring is sized for (4011 against 4014). Every one of the sixteen cases reports
bitwise=OK replay=OK bounds=...:OK over_cap_rejected=OK
.
Both tests spawn one process per GPU themselves, so they need 8 SM90 GPUs and a working NVLink group.

Add a fused SM90 FP8 MegaMoE with a lag-ordered ring schedule
…
cbd08d9
The Hopper MegaMoE runs its two linears as two kernels, so the whole linear-1 activation is written
to the symmetric buffer before linear 2 reads any of it, the two GEMMs cannot overlap, and the pool
grows with the token bound rather than with what the GEMMs have in flight. This adds a single-kernel
path next to it: one task stream in which a per-CTA tile table keeps linear 2 a bounded number of
tiles behind linear 1, with the linear-1 activation pool sized as a ring around that lag, so it only
holds the rows in flight. At the benchmark's 8192-token bound the symmetric buffer goes from 3023 to
700 MiB on 4096/2048/256/top-6 and from 5083 to 1113 MiB on 7168/3072/384/top-6.

The path is additive and opt-in: `fused=True` on the buffer size query allocates the ring buffer and
the buffer type then selects the kernel at launch, so the two-kernel path, its heuristics and its
launcher are untouched and its two Python entry points only gain keyword arguments whose defaults
dispatch exactly as they do today. The query also returns the ring capacity and the lag encoding,
and both travel back to the kernel on every launch together with the K granularity of the
intermediate activation scales (per-128 K where the 256-wide decode tile fits, per-64 K otherwise).
The default layout keeps the full pool below 1024 tokens per rank and rings above it; a caller can
still ask for a ring sized for a given expert wave, or for an automatically chosen one. Decode-sized
calls also take the programmatic dependent launch attribute, since their instantiation carries
griddepcontrol wait/trigger.

Contributor
What
The DSpark paper (Section 3.2.1) calibrates the confidence head with
Sequential Temperature Scaling (STS)
: for each block position, left to right, a 1D grid search picks the temperature that minimizes the ECE of the cumulative prefix-survival probability, keeping the already-fitted earlier positions fixed. The evaluator already measures exactly that quantity (per-position cumulative-product ECE / AUROC / reliability diagrams), but the calibration step itself was missing — and the raw confidence scores are noticeably overconfident.
This PR adds the full offline STS workflow (pure additions, default behavior unchanged):
eval.py --confidence-dump-dir
— dumps per-proposal confidence records to
<dir>/<dataset>/confidence_records.jsonl
for offline fitting (run with
--confidence-threshold 0
and no calibration so the dumped logits are raw and blocks untruncated).
scripts/fit_confidence_calibration.py
— fits per-position temperatures from dumped records via the paper's left-to-right grid search (the ECE binning mirrors the evaluator's coarse bins), and reports cumulative ECE before/after at each position.
eval.py --confidence-calibration-path
— applies the fitted temperatures to the confidence logits during evaluation, so both the reported calibration metrics and the
--confidence-threshold
early stop consume calibrated probabilities.
Validation
Single RTX 4080,
deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7
on
Qwen/Qwen3-4B
, temperature 1.0, threshold 0,
max-new-tokens
256. Fitted on gsm8k (120 samples, 4.7k proposals); held-out datasets were never seen during fitting. Seeds are identical between the two runs, so generation is unchanged and the comparison is purely the calibration:
held-out
cumulative ECE (mean)
AUROC (mean)
alpaca ×100
0.0893 → 0.0315
0.8530 → 0.8516 (unchanged)
mt-bench ×80
0.0697 → 0.0224
0.8693 → 0.8686 (unchanged)
On the fit set (gsm8k) the per-position cumulative ECE drops from 0.031–0.140 to 0.007–0.023. The fitted temperatures are all > 1 (1.28–1.82), matching the paper's overconfidence observation, and the unchanged AUROC confirms the transform is order-preserving.
A synthetic sanity check (prefix labels generated from known per-position probabilities, logits sharpened ×2) recovers T ≈ 2.0 at every position and cuts cumulative ECE by ~90%.

Summary
This PR adds an opt-in, two-stage packed selected-KV sparse decode path for the
GLM-5.2 / V3.2 FP8 MLA format on SM90:
pack_selected_kv
gathers selected records from the paged KV cache into an
opaque tile-major workspace.
flash_mla_with_packed_kvcache
consumes that workspace with a packed
sparse-decode specialization that avoids sparse index and page translation
on the attention critical path.
The existing native sparse-decode API and dispatch remain unchanged. The new
path is explicitly restricted to SM90 and is not enabled automatically.
Note
Alternative host-offload path (not part of this pr):
The packed interface also enables a separate offload path in which gathering and packing are performed on the host, followed by transferring only the packed selected-KV workspace to the device. In this case, the full KV caches of the shared layers no longer need to remain resident in HBM. This can substantially expand KV-cache capacity.
Since this implementation introduces a compile-time packed-KV specialization in the existing SM90 sparse decode kernel, I’d appreciate maintainers’ guidance on whether you prefer the current shared-kernel approach, a policy/loader-based abstraction, or a separate packed-kernel implementation; I’m happy to restructure it in a follow-up revision based on your feedback.
Motivation
GLM-5.2 can share selected physical indices across multiple MLA layers. When
those indices are available before the layer that consumes them, the runtime
can move sparse address resolution and KV gathering into an earlier overlap
window.
The attention kernel can then read a contiguous packed workspace instead of
repeatedly:
loading and validating physical indices;
translating indices into page and in-page coordinates;
constructing unrelated global addresses; and
gathering NoPE, scale, and RoPE components from the paged cache.
Packing and attention are intentionally separate operations so a runtime can
overlap packing with preceding work such as MoE communication.
What changed
SM90 packing kernel
pack_selected_kv
copies each selected 656-byte V3.2 record byte-for-byte:
512-byte FP8 E4M3 NoPE data;
16-byte FP32 scales; and
128-byte BF16 RoPE data.
The packer writes an opaque 64-token tile-major workspace. It supports a valid
selected-index prefix described by
topk_length
and zero-fills invalid suffix
records.
Callers may provide reusable contiguous
uint8
storage using
get_packed_kv_workspace_size
.
Packed attention specialization
The packed H=64 and H=128 instantiations reuse FlashMLA's existing:
WGMMA and dequantization pipeline;
online softmax;
DSM clustering for H=128;
split accumulation;
epilogue; and
combine kernel.
The specialization replaces the sparse index/page/gather loader with direct
tile-major loads and preserves partial-tail masking.
Scheduler policy
H=128 uses the same scheduler as native sparse decode.
H=64 uses the compact request-local scheduler selected by the L20X
experiments. For the measured full-prefix
topk=2048
, 132-SM
B*S_q=16
regime, it falls back to the faster native scheduler.
This scheduler is used only by the opt-in packed helper and does not change
native sparse decode. The benchmark includes an identical-scheduler control to
isolate the packed-load kernel gain.
Python API
This PR adds:
get_packed_kv_workspace_size
get_packed_mla_metadata
pack_selected_kv
flash_mla_with_packed_kvcache
Supported scope
The initial path is intentionally limited to:
SM90;
V3.2 FP8 sparse KV records;
d_qk=576
;
d_v=512
;
H in {64, 128}
;
MQA KV; and
top-k capacity divisible by 64.
The API fails closed for unsupported architectures and shapes. SM100 is not
enabled because this implementation has only been evaluated on SM90.
L20X results
The repository-local benchmark was run on an NVIDIA L20X with 132 SMs using:
CUDA 13.0;
PyTorch 2.13.0;
topk=2048
;
B={1,2,4,7,8}
;
S_q={1,2,3,4,8,16}
;
H={64,128}
;
request-disjoint physical KV ranges;
a 512 MiB L2 flush before each measured path;
10 warmups and 200 timed repetitions; and
60 total cases.
Comparison
Geometric-mean speedup
Wins
Packed attention, identical scheduler
1.098x
60/60
Integrated packed attention stage
1.115x
60/60
Integrated H=64 cohort
1.131x
30/30
H=128 cohort, native scheduler
1.100x
30/30
Pack + attention without overlap
0.740x
0/60
Packing is excluded from the attention-stage comparisons.
The unhidden result is included deliberately: this path is useful only when
the runtime can move most packing work outside the attention critical path.
This PR does not add automatic dispatch or change the default native path.
The H=64 hybrid policy selected the tuned scheduler in 26 cases and the native
fallback in four cases. The four fallback cases improved by approximately
6.5% to 7.4% compared with using the tuned scheduler unconditionally.
Correctness and benchmark coverage
python tests/test_flash_mla_packed_sparse_decoding.py
python benchmark/bench_flash_mla_packed_sparse_decode.py \
  --output packed_sparse_decode_latency.csv
The correctness test passes five cases covering:
a single full boundary tile;
H=64 partial tails and heterogeneous active lengths;
the H=64 native-scheduler fallback;
full production top-k with H=128; and
H=128 heterogeneous partial tails.
The tests compare both output and LSE with native sparse decode and verify the
packed workspace layout.
Observed result:
passed 5 packed sparse-decode cases
The new CUDA kernels compiled for SM90 without register spills. The packer
used 18 registers, and both packed-attention instantiations used 168 registers.
Runtime follow-up
This PR contains the two FlashMLA kernels needed for the packed path, but
intentionally does not include current-token runtime orchestration.
A future vLLM integration can:
pack historical records early into caller-managed storage;
overwrite any selected current-token record after its KV becomes available,
for example with a scatter operation;
synchronize the packing/update stream with attention; and
select native fallback when the expected overlap is insufficient.
Workspace pooling, CUDA stream placement, current-token updates, overlap
eligibility, and end-to-end TPOT measurements belong to that runtime
integration.
For
topk=2048
, the workspace requires approximately 1.281 MiB per query row,
so runtime dispatch should also enforce a workspace budget.
Non-goals
This PR does not:
replace or modify the behavior of native sparse decode;
enable the packed path by default;
add SM100 support;
claim an end-to-end speedup without concurrent runtime integration; or
include current-token patch orchestration.
setup.py
is changed only to register the three new CUDA source files.

Conversation

commented

Copy link

Summary
This PR adds optional per-request
topk_length
support to the SM90
DeepSeek-V3.2 FP8 sparse decode kernel (
d_qk=576
). SM90 V3.2 can now use
dynamic top-k instead of always processing the full allocated top-k capacity.
When
topk_length
is provided, the kernel:
loads the valid length for each batch row;
schedules only
max(ceil_div(topk_length, TOPK_BLOCK_SIZE), 1)
blocks;
masks a partial tail before its indices can be used for KV addressing; and
includes the absolute top-k position in the softmax validity predicate.
When
topk_length == nullptr
, the existing fixed top-k behavior is preserved.
There is no public API change, and MODEL1 and SM100 behavior are unchanged.
Why
template<bool DYNAMIC_TOPK, ...>
I also tested a single-device-kernel implementation that checks
params.topk_length != nullptr
at runtime. The condition is grid-uniform, but
the compiler cannot remove the length load, tail predicates, extra control
flow, or their value lifetimes from the fixed path.
template<bool DYNAMIC_TOPK>
moves the choice to host launch dispatch:
false
: the dynamic-length logic is compiled out, preserving the fixed path;
true
: per-row block counts and partial-tail safety checks are enabled.

title: fix(responses): preserve plaintext Codex agent messages
body:
Codex uses Responses `agent_message` input items for agent-to-agent tasks, messages, and completion reports. Recipe currently deserializes them as `Unsupported` and silently discards them during conversion. An otherwise valid request containing only such an item therefore produces an empty conversation, and mixed histories lose the task or result before prompt rendering.

Add explicit support in the shared Rust Responses converter, so both Rust callers and Python bindings preserve plaintext agent input as user messages with sender and recipient attribution. Join text blocks in order with newlines, following Codex's plaintext content handling, and use the existing message path and tool-call validation. Reject empty, malformed, encrypted, mixed encrypted/plaintext, or non-text agent input rather than silently dropping or partially forwarding it. Agent text and attribution also follow the existing image-placeholder validation.

This supports the plaintext Codex input extension; it does not perform agent routing or decrypt content. The existing behavior of unrelated unsupported input types is preserved.

Minimal reproduction with the current Python package (no model or credentials needed):

```python
from deepseek_recipe import ConversionOptions, ResponsesRequest

converted = ResponsesRequest({
    "model": "test-model",
    "input": [{
        "type": "agent_message",
        "author": "/root",
        "recipient": "/root/worker",
        "content": [{"type": "input_text", "text": "NEW_TASK marker_92714"}],
    }],
}).convert(ConversionOptions())
print([message.content for message in converted.conversation.messages])
```

Before: `[]`. After: one user message containing the attribution and `NEW_TASK marker_92714`.

The input shape and plaintext block joining are defined in [Codex's protocol models](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.159.3/codex-rs/protocol/src/models.rs#L908).

Validation:

- The new Rust regression suite fails on the original main branch (6 failures; the unrelated unsupported-item compatibility case still passes). The new Python cases also fail against the published 0.1.1 package (5 failures).
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test --workspace --locked` — 23 tests pass, including 7 new converter regressions covering task/message/result ordering, tool history, malformed or unreadable content, and image-placeholder validation.
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS='-D warnings' cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --locked`
- Built the Python bindings from this branch with `maturin develop --manifest-path deepseek-recipe-python/Cargo.toml --locked`, then ran `python -m pytest deepseek-recipe-python/tests server-py/tests` — 36 tests pass, including rendered prompt/tokenization checks and streaming/non-streaming HTTP checks that reject unreadable input before inference.

The tests use synthetic messages and require no model endpoint or credentials.

title: Fix JSON stream output across chunk boundaries
body:
## Summary

- make JSON-mode response text independent of how inference text is split into source chunks
- ignore empty text chunks in the parser while still counting their backend token usage
- add regression coverage for every UTF-8 character boundary, one-character chunks, and empty chunks

## Problem

Outside a detected JSON value, the state machine replaces unmatched text with whitespace so the result remains valid JSON. `StashedChunks` currently emits one space for every backing inference chunk, however. The same model text therefore produces different response content when a backend changes only its chunk boundaries.

On unmodified `8cadfede7063c896b944e7bae05daa3549ae97ea`, the new test fails when the JSON prefix is split after its first character: the split stream produces two leading spaces while the single-chunk stream produces one. An empty text chunk can add another space for the same reason.

The fix emits whitespace once per contiguous `ToSpace` region and keeps empty text out of the parser. Completion-token accounting remains unchanged.

## Testing

Using the repository-pinned Rust 1.97.1 toolchain:

```text
cargo test -p deepseek-recipe --locked
# 2 integration tests passed; doc-tests passed

cargo clippy -p deepseek-recipe --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all -- --check
git diff --check origin/main...HEAD
```

The chunk-invariance test compares a single inference chunk against every valid UTF-8 split point and a stream with one chunk per character. The empty-chunk test also verifies that five completion tokens are retained while response content stays exactly ` {"ok":true} `.

## Scope

This changes only streamed output normalization in JSON mode. It does not change JSON detection, stop-sequence matching, tool-call parsing, protocol schemas, or inference behavior.

title: Add locked Rust workspace CI
body:
## Summary

Add two read-only CI jobs using the repository's pinned Rust toolchain and `Cargo.lock`:

- Core: formatting, protocol/encoding crate tests, and the image crate without native preprocessing.
- Full workspace: Clippy with warnings denied, workspace tests including doctests, and rustdoc with warnings denied.

Refreshed onto v0.2.0 (`935817c`). Its animated-image path needs OpenCV >=4.11, so the full job builds minimal OpenCV 4.12 from pinned commit `49486f61fb25722cbcf586b7f4320921d46fb38e` rather than relying on the runner's distro version. Only core/imgproc/imgcodecs and the required codecs are enabled; CUDA, GUI, video and tests are disabled. The private prefix is exposed to both native linking and doctest runtime loading. No Rust source is changed.

## Validation

On an independent Linux host, against unchanged `935817c` source with Rust 1.97.1:

- Built the exact proposed OpenCV build script and generated the real Rust bindings.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: passed.
- `cargo check -p deepseek-recipe-image --no-default-features --locked --offline`: passed.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked --offline -- -D warnings`: passed.
- `cargo test --workspace --locked --offline`: **100 unit tests and 1 doctest passed**, none failed or skipped.
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --locked --offline`: passed.
- YAML parsing and Bash syntax checks passed for all 11 run blocks.

Dependencies were fetched once before the native checks, which then reused a private offline Cargo cache. This validates the command set and native library setup, not a GitHub-hosted workflow run or the runner's apt/actions installation. Hosted CI remains to be exercised. No Python wheel, model inference, GPU, performance or cross-platform claim.

AI-assisted contribution; validation and limitations are reported above.

title: perf(cake_msa): persistent heavy-first union prefill, streaming Top-K merge/scan (rounds 11-15 re-export)
body:
The Cake-generated MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA) kernels for Blackwell in FlashInfer ship 31 route variants on each of sm_100a and sm_103a: 9 decode routes, 12 prefill union routes (bf16/bf16, bf16-q/fp8-kv and fp16/fp16, flat and paged), 6 long-context bf16 reverse prefill routes (main and reduce passes), and 4 Top-K select routes. This PR delivers new program versions for 9 of these routes per architecture and adds or removes no route. The bf16/bf16 union prefill routes flat gqa16, flat gqa8, paged gqa16 (any, causal_large, causal_mask64) and paged gqa8 run a persistent heavy-first tile loop over GQA-folded tiles, the two bf16-q/fp8-kv gqa0 union prefill routes gain only a shared-memory proxy fence, and `topk_select_streaming` uses an 8-warp rank-count merge and a shared-memory-staged scan row. title: perf(cake_msa): faster Blackwell MSA uniform-FP8 decode and Top-K programs — epilogue overlap and QK ahead of PV (D-U1, D-U2, D-U2b), streaming Top-K merge network (S2), tradix v2 radix layout, per-architecture topk_select (CAKE-1183 round 10)
body:
> Developed by the **CAKE team**, this PR re-exports the Cake-generated MiniMax Sparse Attention family for SM100 / SM103 with the CAKE-1183 levers accepted in rounds 9-10 that are not yet on `main`.
> Two route groups change: uniform-FP8 decode (D-U1, D-U2, D-U2b) and Top-K select (S2, tradix v2, per-architecture `topk_select`). Prefill routes do not change. This is one commit directly on `main` `fb83b0ee` and is not stacked.
> No lever changes the arithmetic. Outputs and Top-K indices are bitwise identical in every Cake A/B.
> Speedup vs the reference kernels (vllm-project/MSA `dev` @ `968061ab`, `fmha_sm100`), same job, geomean (min-max):
>
> | rows | GB300 (sm_103a) | B200 (sm_100a) |
> |---|---|---|
> | FP8 decode, 14 rows (12 uniform-FP8 q8 + 2 legacy q1) | **1.747×** (1.511-4.473) | **1.619×** (1.374-4.586) |
> | uniform-FP8 q8 decode alone, 12 rows | 1.511-1.554× | 1.374-1.423× |
> | Top-K, 9 of 10 rows (with a reference route) | **2.404×** (1.296-5.257) | **2.358×** (1.323-5.493) |

## Summary

This PR regenerates the family in `csrc/blackwell_msa/` and `flashinfer/jit/blackwell_msa.py`. The host file `flashinfer/msa_ops/_blackwell_sm100.py` is regenerated byte-identical to `main`. The source is Cake producer `951efcee` (CAKE-1183 MSA ceiling round 10), and the target is FlashInfer `main` `fb83b0ee`. The export changes 46 uniform-FP8 decode routes and 11 Top-K routes. The 59 prefill routes, the other 54 decode routes and the other 5 Top-K routes are identical. The exporter now traces `topk_select` per architecture, so sm_100a gets its own unpadded layout.

Linear: CAKE-1183.

## What changed

Route diff of the export protocol against the round-9 prefill protocol:

| route group / program | lever (Cake MR) | mechanism (details below) | launch SMEM, bytes |
|---|---|---|---|
| uniform-FP8 decode (46 routes) | D-U1, D-U2, D-U2b (!1445) | The item epilogue overlaps the next item's first QK. QK(pair+1) issues before PV(pair), with P in two SMEM tiles and a `p_free` barrier. Correction waits on `p_free` before each TMEM rescale. | `dynamic_smem_bytes` 183296 → 216064 (the two P tiles of D-U2) |
| Top-K streaming `topk_select_streaming` | S2 (!1439) | A warp-local bitonic top-16 merge replaces 16 CTA-wide argmax rounds. | 33024 → 33792 |
| Top-K radix `topk_select` | tradix v2 (!1439) + exporter change | Bank-disjoint segment visits. Padded strides on sm_103a only. One program per architecture. | sm_100a 75520 (unpadded); sm_103a 75520 → 75648 |
| Top-K radix `topk_select_keq` | tradix v2 (!1439) | Bank-disjoint segment visits and padded strides. | 75520 → 75648 (both architectures) |
| Top-K radix `topk_select_q32` | tradix v2 (!1439) | Bank-disjoint segment visits, padded strides and rank index `q_local + 16·w`. | 85376 → 85632 |
| prefill (59 routes) | none | unchanged | unchanged |

**D-U1.** Before this change, the MMA warp waited for correction's `decode_done` before it issued item k+1. Now the wait sits between item k+1's QK(0)/QK(1) and its first PV, so the epilogue overlaps the next item's first QK. Only the last item of a CTA keeps the end-of-item wait.

**D-U2.** Softmax now writes P as E4M3 into two 128B-swizzled K-major SMEM tiles, guarded by a new `p_free` barrier. Before, P aliased part of the FP32 score tile in TMEM. The MMA warp now issues QK(pair+1) before PV(pair), so the next softmax step overlaps PV(pair).

**D-U2b.** QK-ahead order removes the implicit "PV(s, p−1) is done" edge that `s_full(p)` used to carry. Correction therefore now waits on `p_free[s]` before the TMEM rescale of pair >= 1. The 4-stage KV ring (sm_100a) exposes the race. The sm_103a text carried the same latent race, so D-U2b is in both texts.

**S2.** Each of the 8 warps selects its local top-16 with a bitonic network (`_merge_warp_top16`), and warp 0 merges the 8 × 16 candidates with the same network. This replaces 16 rounds of CTA-wide argmax. Ties break by index, the same as in the reference, and dynamic barriers per CTA drop from 19 to 2.

**Tradix v2.** Odd segments are visited as `j ^ (seg & 1)`, so the two half-warps no longer alias banks. The candidate stride is padded from 64 to 65 u64 and the output-count stride from 16 to 17. The padding is applied per instance and per architecture, and the sm_100a stage-only k64 `topk_select` instance keeps the unpadded stride. On sm_100a, `topk_select_keq` compiles to 127 registers (base 75, 0 spill) and its production shapes go from 3 to 2 CTAs/SM; Cake accepted this because no row regresses beyond the band on either architecture.

**Per-architecture `topk_select`.** This is an exporter change, not a kernel change. Tradix v2 pads `topk_select` on sm_103a only, so `_build("topk", arch)` now traces it per architecture and emits `cake_blackwell_msa_c14b5fe5d3aa9f47ab07` [sm_100a] and `cake_blackwell_msa_f35ca4f807d8df7077ed` [sm_103a]. `topk_select_keq` and `topk_select_q32` stay one program for both architectures, and the FlashInfer loader does not change.

**Not in this PR.** The producer's three NVFP4 decode levers (N9a-2, C2 short-epilogue, N8a v2) belong to the separately exported NVFP4 decode family, and no NVFP4 program is in the delivered files.

## Precision

The delivered levers change scheduling, barrier placement, SMEM layout or the location of P. They do not change the arithmetic. The Cake A/Bs of all delivered levers are bitwise, and the levers make no change to dtype, tolerance, selected-block set or public signature. The export protocol's correctness check against the FP32 reference passes on all 88 GB300 shapes.

## Speedup vs the reference kernels

The reference is vllm-project/MSA `dev` @ `968061ab` (`fmha_sm100`), using the fastest admissible reference route per row: `msa_decode_csrc` or `msa_decode_cute_csr` for decode, and `msa_topk_hkt` or `msa_topk_thk` for Top-K. The Cake arm runs this PR's kernel texts (Cake tree `0585a6d4`) through the Cake dispatcher. Both arms ran in the same job per architecture: one GB300 job (JHB) and one B200 job (NSC), both on 2026-10-17. Timing uses FlashInfer's `bench_gpu_time` in strict CUPTI mode with a cold L2, 11 timed samples after 5 warm-up calls and two passes. Every (row, arm) correctness check passed. Ratio = reference median / Cake median; above 1 means Cake is faster.

| rows | GB300 (sm_103a), geomean (min-max) | B200 (sm_100a), geomean (min-max) |

| FP8 decode, 14 rows (12 uniform-FP8 q8 + 2 legacy q1) | **1.747×** (1.511-4.473) | **1.619×** (1.374-4.586) |

| Top-K, 9 of 10 rows (with a reference route) | **2.404×** (1.296-5.257) | **2.358×** (1.323-5.493) |

On the four `topk_thk_*` rows it runs on the HKT view of the same scores, while the reference runs its faster THK path, so those ratios are conservative for Cake.

## Validation

On the GB300 leg, all 88 / 88 shapes are correct: 78 pass all gates and 10 fail timing gates only. On the B200 leg, all 87 / 87 shapes are correct: 76 pass all gates and 11 fail timing gates only. Rows that are correct and fail only timing-validity gates are accepted under the same rule as #6397 / #6410 / #6443 / #6459 / #6463. title: fix(moe): make the trtllm-gen BMM default config independent of manifest order
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

The untuned default config of the trtllm-gen batched GEMM (`getDefaultValidConfigIndex`, used by every trtllm-gen MoE call without autotuning) is the first entry of `getValidConfigIndices()`, sorted with `std::sort`. The comparator only compared tileK / unroll / tileM / tileN / scheduler, so many configs tied, and `std::sort` ordered the ties by its input, i.e. by the cubin manifest. #6726 only reordered pre-existing kernels in `flashinferMetaInfo.h`, and that moved the default onto slower tie-mates:

- NVFP4 FC2 (`m=1 n=8192 k=1280`): the unsplit `c1x1x1` kernel (0.071 ms) was replaced by its `splitK3` tie-mate (0.135 ms). The `splitK2` tie-mate takes 0.095 ms.
- MXFP4 x MXFP8 FC1 (DeepSeek-V4 shapes): the `s6 c2x1x1` kernel (0.631 ms) was replaced by its `s3 c1x1x1` tie-mate (0.718 ms).

Separately, the scheduler tier estimated `numCtas` from `idx0` only, and that estimate includes split-K and clusters. As a result `cmp(a, b)` and `cmp(b, a)` could disagree. With Static / Persistent / Persistent-split-K tie-mates near the SM count this forms a cycle, so the comparator was not a strict weak ordering, and split-K could still be the default in an input-order-dependent way.

This PR makes the order total and manifest-independent:

1. **Prefer fewer `mNumSlicesForSplitK` slices**, placed before the scheduler tier. Split-K is still a candidate for the autotuner, which receives the full list.
2. **Make the scheduler tier symmetric.** Its CTA estimate drops split-K and clusters, so it depends only on the tile shape, which both sides share at that tier. The tier also only decides Persistent vs non-Persistent.
3. **Prefer deeper A/B pipelines** (`mNumStagesA`, then `mNumStagesB`).
4. **Break the remaining ties with `strcmp(mFunctionName)`**, which is unique per manifest. Neither `std::stable_sort` nor a tie-break on the config index would help, because both still follow manifest order.

Only configs that the existing tiers left tied change order.

### Performance (untuned default, `--autotune` off)

title: fix(experimental/b12x): deterministic DSA-indexer top-k tie-break
body:
## 📌 Description

The DSA indexer's radix-select top-k assigned output slots to tied candidates via shared-memory atomics (`_smem_xadd`) in nondeterministic thread order. Identical prompts could therefore select different read plans across runs, changing attention outputs: we measured a 27–31% coherence-flake rate on a 32K verbatim-recall canary (graph-, cache-, MoE-, sampling-independent) under a production serving profile.

Fix: perturb the radix-select **key** by `candidate_index * 2^-24` (`_TIE_BREAK_EPS`), so ties resolve by candidate index deterministically. Output score values are untouched. Applied at:

- `flashinfer/experimental/b12x/attention/dsa_indexer/fused_indexer.py`: `_fused_radix_select` (4 sites) + cooperative grid-barrier merge path.
- `flashinfer/experimental/b12x/attention/dsa_indexer/tiled_topk.py`: all 8 radix sites + `_exact_overflow_fallback(tie_break_self)`.

A host-side variant that perturbed output values was reverted upstream of the port (not ported).

Source: port of archived `local-inference-lab/b12x` commit `59548d5429a59bc869aa7d61cfef9a8486114171` (authorship preserved). The archived repo is read-only; this is the port per its migration guide.

## 🔍 Related Issues

Tracking issue: #6735

## Results (port base vs port, same benchmark and hardware)

- Determinism: 20/20 repeated top-k runs reduce to 1 distinct selected set (was nondeterministic run-to-run on tied inputs).
- Correctness: 246 archived-b12x indexer tests pass on the archived base; the ported determinism suites cover the fused and tiled paths on SM120.
- Serving: 32K canary ×10 = 10/10 PASS (was 27–31% flake), TP2+DCP2 MTP3 profile, GLM-5.3-Flash, 2× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (96 GiB, SM120), driver 615.71.09, Arch Linux kernel 7.2.8-arch1-2, clocks locked 2200 MHz (LACT), 275 W power cap.
