title: fix(autotuner): rank BF16 cute-dsl tactics on a cold launch chain
body:
## 📌 Description

`mm_bf16(backend="cute-dsl")` autotuning ranked low-M tactics by **isolated single-launch latency** rather than the cold-L2 chained cost it was configured for, and picked measurably slower tactics than ones in its own candidate set. `backend="auto"`, which has included the cute-dsl runners since #6392, had the same problem and also ranked them against cuDNN, TGV and TinyGEMM on isolated launches.

**Root cause.** #4908 added `TuningConfig.use_cold_l2_graph_replay` for the BF16 cute-dsl config: rank tactics on a graph of launches, each with its own input copy, timed after an L2 flush. #4361 then routed every `use_cold_l2_cache=True` config to `cold_l2_profile`, which times one graph launch per flushed sample, so the flag stopped having any effect. A single isolated launch carries a ~6.3 µs floor on B300 (a trivial `add_` measures 6.38 µs) plus a first-launch cost that differs by kernel family (cluster split-K > warp split-K > direct). The real kernels take 2.8–6.4 µs, so candidates tied at ~10.24 µs and the pick came down to noise. Neither the event timer (32 ns resolution) nor PDL (same with `pdl=False`) causes it.

**Changes**
- `cold_l2_profile`: with `use_cuda_graph` and `use_cold_l2_graph_replay`, capture all profile-arena iterations as one graph and report the median sample divided by the launch count. Without a profile arena the graph keeps its single launch, so the MXFP8 cute-dsl config (which sets the flag but has no arena) is unchanged.
- `pure_profile`: remove the cold-L2 replay/eviction branch, unreachable since #4361 sends every cold-L2 config to `cold_l2_profile`.
- `ValueProfileArena` accepts non-overlapping dense permuted views (e.g. the `W.T` weight) by keeping strides on its lane views.
- Dedicated BF16 cute-dsl config, selected whenever the cute-dsl runners compete (`backend="cute-dsl"`, or `backend="auto"` when cute-dsl is a suitable candidate): `profiling_repeat=32` and the weight in the profile arena. The weight cycles through two ≥2×L2 arenas (2 × 265 MB on B300), and the 40 MB workspace stays shared; 32 full input clones would need ~4.4 GB at N=19456 K=2560. A 10-launch chain still tied or flipped split-K vs warp split-K at N=512 K=8192 M=16; 32 launches ranked all probed tactics in harness order across 3 trials.
- Under `auto`, every candidate runner (cuDNN, CUTLASS, TGV, TinyGEMM, cuBLASLt and the cute-dsl runners) is ranked on the same cold chain. The cute-dsl requirement (column-major contiguous weight) guarantees the dense weight the arena needs.
- Runner sets without cute-dsl (explicit cuDNN/CUTLASS/TGV/cuBLASLt/TinyGEMM, or `auto` with a non-column-major weight) keep the shared config and isolated timing with the original input tensors. This preserves cuDNN support for padded/gapped weight strides, which the dense profile arena rejects.
- `_profiling_policy` reports `cold-chain` for chained configs, so persisted picks from the isolated measurement are re-ranked.

## 📊 Performance

B300 SXM (sm_103), CUDA 13.0, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0, `pdl=True`. Harness: rotate ≥2 GiB of distinct weight buffers inside one CUDA graph (cold L2), time with CUDA events over replays, arms in ABAB order; values are median µs per GEMM. Baseline is unpatched `main` (f63b2e7cb).

| tuned vs hand, geomean | 1.017× | **1.124×** |
| cells where tuned loses >5% to hand | 17 (worst 0.719×) | **0** (worst 0.983×) |
| tuned vs cuBLAS, geomean | 1.741× | 1.915× |
| tuned this PR vs tuned main, geomean | — | 1.108× |

Largest changes:

| (M, N, K) | cuBLAS | hand | main tuned | PR tuned |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (1, 512, 8192) | 5.37 | 2.79 | 3.88 | **2.75** |
| (8, 512, 8192) | 5.84 | 3.68 | 5.02 | **3.68** |

**`backend="auto"`.** GB300 (sm_103), CUDA 13.0, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0, same cold-L2 harness. Five shapes (N, K) ∈ {(256, 8192), (512, 8192), (3584, 2560), (2560, 1536), (19456, 2560)} × M ∈ {1, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32}, one tuning run per arm. Each cell is compared with the fastest of five tuning arms (cute-dsl and auto, each under isolated, cold-chain or CUPTI-span timing; geomean):

Ranking by CUPTI kernel spans removes the launch floor but still prefers warp split-K where split-K is 1.2–1.4× faster (pdl=1 geomean 1.072×), so it is not a substitute for the chain.

title: [Core][DP] Prefix-affinity tie-break in the internal DP load balancer
body:
## Purpose

Partial mitigation for #52463: the tie-break rotation added in #47420 degrades prefix-cache locality for multi-turn / shared-prefix traffic under the internal DP load balancer. Consecutive turns of one conversation are tied decisions at low load, so they rotate across DP ranks and every turn misses the prefix its previous turn cached.

This PR remembers which engine served a prompt's first-block prefix (LRU of 16k entries, keyed on `cache_salt` + LoRA id + first `block_size` prompt token ids) and prefers that engine **only when scores tie**:

- Load-aware decisions unchanged — a lower-scored engine always wins.
- Unrelated tied requests still rotate — #47420's fairness fix is preserved (regression-tested).
- Explicit `data_parallel_rank` and late-interaction routing bypass affinity, unchanged.
- Stale entries from elastic-EP scale-in are discarded; sub-block prompts (which cannot hit the cache) are exempt.

## Test Plan

- `tests/v1/engine/test_dp_lb_prefix_affinity.py` — 8 CPU-only unit tests driving `get_core_engine_for_request` directly: session stickiness across turns, tied-unrelated rotation preserved, load-beats-affinity, sub-block exemption, cache_salt separation, explicit-rank bypass, scale-in staleness, LRU bound.
- Hardware A/B on 8×H100 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, DP=4+EP, `--api-server-count 4`, fp8 KV, aiperf mooncake trace designed for 81.7% prefix reuse — full methodology in #52463): identical runs, only this patch differs.

## Test Result

Unit: 8/8 pass (run inside `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` image).

Hardware A/B (prefix-cache hit rate, per-user output tok/s):

| conc | hit rate before → after | tok/s/user before → after |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 37.6% → **61.5%** | 69.5 → 73.6 (+6%) |
| 4 | 52.9% → 53.5% | 47.2 → 45.1 (−4%) |
| 16 | 20.0% → 21.9% | 16.3 → 12.6 (−23%)* |
| 32 | 16.0% → **23.2%** | 9.7 → 9.6 (−1%) |
| 64 | 10.9% → 11.1% | 5.0 → 4.8 (−5%) |
| 128 | 7.8% → 8.8% | 2.6 → 2.7 (+4%) |

\* hit rate unchanged while throughput moved — consistent with run-to-run variance at 160 requests/level, not a cache effect; happy to re-run if reviewers want more samples.

**Known limitation (why this is a mitigation, not the full fix):** with `--api-server-count N` each frontend process has its own client and affinity map, and SO_REUSEPORT spreads one session's connections across processes — client-side affinity only sees its own process's requests (this bounds the c=1 recovery at 61.5% vs 81.6% measured on v0.23.0, a pre-#47420 release — a version-level baseline, not a single-commit revert of #47420). The complete fix needs prefix-awareness at a shared layer (DP coordinator or a shared affinity table); #52463 is the home for that design discussion.

FIX #52463

title: [Bug][DP] Tie-break rotation from #47420 degrades prefix-cache locality for multi-turn traffic under internal DP LB
body:
### Your current environment

vLLM nightly `ac7509e2b1db` (also reproduced on the latest release build), 8×H100 SXM (one node), `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`, `--data-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel --api-server-count 4 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --max-model-len 1000000 --block-size 256`, prefix caching enabled (default).

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**#47420 ("Rotate load-balancer tie-break to avoid systematic engine bias") degrades prefix-cache locality for multi-turn / shared-prefix traffic under internal DP load balancing.**

`DPLBAsyncMPClient.get_core_engine_for_request` resolves score ties by scanning from `eng_start_index`, and since #47420 that start index rotates after every decision. A multi-turn conversation at low load is exactly a stream of tied decisions, so consecutive turns rotate across DP ranks — and every turn misses the prefix its previous turn left in that rank's KV cache. Before #47420 the fixed scan start accidentally pinned each frontend client's tied decisions to one rank, which is what kept sessions cache-local.

Measured with an aiperf mooncake-trace replay matched to production shape (multi-turn sessions, ~34k-token prompts, trace designed for **81.7%** prefix reuse), identical client and trace on both engines:

| | prefix-cache hit rate (c=1 … c=128) | designed |
|---|---|---|
| v0.23.0 (pre-#47420) | **81.6%** measured run-wide | 81.7% |
| current main (`ac7509e2b1db`) | **37.6% / 52.9% / 20.0% / 16.0% / 10.9% / 7.8%** | 81.7% |

Per-rank counters confirm the mechanism: at c=1 (strictly sequential turns), `vllm:prefix_cache_queries` spreads *evenly* across all 4 DP ranks (~350k each) while hits concentrate on the ranks that happened to repeat.

**On attribution.** The mechanism is confirmed directly: #47420's only behavioral change to `get_core_engine_for_request` is rotating `eng_start_index` per decision, and a tie-break-only A/B on a single nightly (nothing else changed) moves the c=1 hit rate 37.6% → 61.5%. The 81.6% row above is v0.23.0 — a version-level baseline spanning many commits, not a single-commit revert — so it *bounds* rather than *isolates* #47420's exact share; reverting only #47420 on the current nightly would isolate it cleanly. Either way the `--api-server-count` / SO_REUSEPORT factor noted below is an independent contributor.

End-to-end cost on this workload: **−2% to −13% per-user output throughput vs v0.23.0** despite main being +6–17% faster on a cache-defeating random-token ladder (same hardware, same recipe) — the re-prefill of ~34k-token prompts swamps the decode-side wins.

#47420's own benchmark ran with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`, so the fairness fix never saw this cost. The fairness problem it fixed was real; the tie-break just shouldn't rotate *related* requests away from their cache.

### Partial mitigation (PR incoming) and why the full fix needs a design decision

PR from this account: remember which engine served a prompt's first-block prefix (small LRU keyed on `cache_salt` + LoRA id + first `block_size` prompt token ids) and prefer that engine **only when scores tie**. Load-aware decisions are unchanged; unrelated tied requests still rotate, preserving #47420's fairness.

A/B on the hardware above (same trace, same engine, only the tie-break differs): c=1 hit rate 37.6% → **61.5%** (+6% per-user throughput), c=32 16.0% → 23.2%. It does **not** restore the 81.6% baseline, for a structural reason: with `--api-server-count N`, each frontend process has its own `DPLBAsyncMPClient` (and now its own affinity map), and SO_REUSEPORT spreads one session's connections across processes — client-side affinity can only see the requests that land on its process. The pre-#47420 behavior dodged this by pinning *every* client's ties to a per-client rank, at the cost of the fairness bias #47420 fixed.

A complete fix needs prefix-awareness at a shared layer — the DP coordinator, or a shared affinity table across frontend processes — which is a design decision for the maintainers. Filing this issue so the tie-break mitigation and that larger conversation have a home.

--- a/vllm/v1/engine/core_client.py

@@ -7,7 +7,7 @@

-from collections import Counter, defaultdict

@@ -1431,6 +1431,12 @@ def get_core_engine_for_request(self, request: EngineCoreRequest):
         return self.core_engine
 
 
+# Cap on remembered prefix->engine affinities; oldest entries are evicted.
+# 16k entries is a few hundred KiB and covers far more concurrent
+# conversations than a single frontend process realistically serves.
+PREFIX_AFFINITY_LRU_SIZE = 16 * 1024
+
+
 class DPLBAsyncMPClient(DPAsyncMPClient):
     """Asyncio-compatible client for multi-proc, multi-engine (data parallel)
     EngineCore. Load-balances between multiple engine processes."""
@@ -1468,6 +1474,30 @@ def __init__(
             len(self.core_engines) * self.client_index
         ) // client_count
 
+        # Prefix-affinity memory: hash of a request's first-block prompt
+        # prefix -> engine index that most recently served that prefix.
+        # Consulted only to break score ties, so multi-turn conversations and
+        # shared-prefix request families keep landing on the engine that
+        # already holds their prefix in KV cache, while unrelated tied
+        # requests still rotate and load-aware decisions are unaffected.
+        self.prefix_affinity: OrderedDict[int, int] = OrderedDict()
+
+    def _prefix_affinity_key(self, request: EngineCoreRequest) -> int | None:
+        """Affinity key for prefix-cache locality, or None when the request
+        cannot hit the prefix cache (embeds input, or fewer prompt tokens
+        than one KV block)."""
+        tokens = request.prompt_token_ids
+        block_size = self.vllm_config.cache_config.block_size
+        if (
+            not tokens
+            or len(tokens) < block_size
+            or request.prompt_embeds is not None
+            or request.prompt_is_token_ids is not None
+        ):
+            return None
+        lora_id = request.lora_request.lora_int_id if request.lora_request else None
+        return hash((request.cache_salt, lora_id, tuple(tokens[:block_size])))
+
     def get_core_engine_for_request(self, request: EngineCoreRequest) -> EngineIdentity:
         # Engines are in rank order.
         if (eng_index := request.data_parallel_rank) is None and (
@@ -1478,6 +1508,14 @@ def get_core_engine_for_request(self, request: EngineCoreRequest) -> EngineIdent
             current_counts = self.lb_engines
             # TODO use P2C alg for larger DP sizes
             num_engines = len(current_counts)
+            affinity_key = self._prefix_affinity_key(request)
+            affinity_index: int | None = None
+            if affinity_key is not None:
+                affinity_index = self.prefix_affinity.get(affinity_key)
+                if affinity_index is not None and affinity_index >= num_engines:
+                    # Engine count shrank since the entry was recorded
+                    # (elastic EP scale-in); the mapping is stale.
+                    affinity_index = None
             min_score: float = sys.maxsize
             eng_index = 0
             for i in range(num_engines):
@@ -1502,7 +1540,11 @@ def get_core_engine_for_request(self, request: EngineCoreRequest) -> EngineIdent
                     # the penalty stays off, preserving exact round-robin.
                     # Ramps from 0 at <=50% usage to 3x waiting at 100%.
                     score += waiting * 6.0 * max(0.0, kv_cache_usage - 0.5)
-                if score < min_score:
+                # Prefer the engine that already holds this request's prefix
+                # in KV cache when it ties on score: recomputing a shared
+                # prefix elsewhere costs a full prefill, spreading ties across
+                # engines saves nothing.
+                if score < min_score or (score == min_score and idx == affinity_index):
                     min_score = score
                     eng_index = idx
             # Increment local waiting count for better balancing between stats
@@ -1512,8 +1554,15 @@ def get_core_engine_for_request(self, request: EngineCoreRequest) -> EngineIdent
             # after a coordinator stats reset when engines look equally loaded)
             # don't systematically favor the same engine. This removes the
             # fixed tie-break bias without affecting load-aware decisions when
-            # scores actually differ.
+            # scores actually differ. Requests with a remembered prefix are
+            # exempt from the rotation (they stick to their engine on ties);
+            # everything else still spreads evenly.
             self.eng_start_index = (self.eng_start_index + 1) % num_engines
+            if affinity_key is not None:
+                self.prefix_affinity[affinity_key] = eng_index
+                self.prefix_affinity.move_to_end(affinity_key)
+                if len(self.prefix_affinity) > PREFIX_AFFINITY_LRU_SIZE:

         chosen_engine = self.core_engines[eng_index]

title: [ROCm][CI] Handle tied experts in softplus sqrt top-k test
body:
- Uses a stable descending sort in the shared PyTorch reference so equal scores resolve to lower expert IDs, matching the CUDA/ROCm and DeepSeek-V4 kernels.
- Makes top-k cutoff ties an explicit regression case by setting the first real gating row to all zeros instead of relying on accidental low-precision collisions.
- Leaves hash routing unchanged and preserves the existing exact expert-ID, weight, padding, and NaN assertions.

[`torch.topk`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.topk.html) does not guarantee which indices it returns for tied elements, while the vLLM kernels deterministically prefer lower expert IDs. The padding test can therefore report a false expert-ID mismatch when BF16 routing scores tie at the top-k cutoff. The failure has consistently appeared in 384-expert BF16 cases as a single mismatched expert ID with an absolute delta of 115:
- [AMD CI #11834, MI355 MoE Test 3](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/11834#019fdfcf-a69f-439e-a7bf-a35ce8955218)
- [AMD CI #11845, MI355 MoE Test 2](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/11845#019fe374-ac4a-4f92-bad5-9620658cf9a5)
- [AMD CI #11862, MI355 MoE Test 3](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/11862#019fe4e5-8e16-4f8e-b421-bd548b93dcf5)
- [AMD CI #12302, MI355 MoE Kernels Shard 2](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/12302#01a0225d-3661-44c5-bae3-ed570d36a9a2)
- [AMD CI #12307, MI355 MoE Kernels Shard 2](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/12307#01a02500-419a-4007-b963-dcc3114443cc)

Using `torch.argsort(..., descending=True, stable=True)` makes the reference follow the kernels' intentional tie-break and keeps exact routing validation rather than treating tied experts as interchangeable.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Describe the bug

  The V1 engine core silently deadlocks under concurrent load using default configuration. The API server remains healthy (/health returns 200, /metrics responds), but zero tokens are generated. Requests stay in "running" state indefinitely and
   the engine never recovers without a pod restart.

  vLLM serve command:
```
  vllm serve "$MODEL_DIR" \
      --tokenizer Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B \
      --dtype bfloat16 \
      --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \
      --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 \
      --max-model-len 16384 \
      --max-num-seqs 128 \
      --quantization fp8 \
      --trust-remote-code \
      --enable-prefix-caching \
      --async-scheduling \
      --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": false}'
```

  How to reproduce:

  1. Deploy vLLM with the configuration above
  2. Send concurrent requests (8-64 concurrency) — works fine initially
  3. Under sustained load or after a brief spike, the engine freezes
  4. No specific error triggers it — no OOM, no CUDA error, no validation error

  Engine log sequence showing the deadlock:
```
  13:57:45  Avg prompt throughput: 2598.6 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 1684.2 tokens/s, Running: 2 reqs, Waiting: 0 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 0.3%, Prefix cache hit rate: 96.9%
  13:57:55  Avg prompt throughput: 83.6 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 1.8 tokens/s, Running: 11 reqs, Waiting: 0 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 1.3%, Prefix cache hit rate: 96.9%
  13:58:05  Avg prompt throughput: 0.0 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 0.0 tokens/s, Running: 11 reqs, Waiting: 0 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 1.3%, Prefix cache hit rate: 96.9%
```
  After 13:58:05, throughput stays at 0.0 permanently. Running count stays at 11. KV cache stays at 1.3%. The engine never recovers.

### Key observations:

  - Not resource exhaustion: Only 11/128 request slots used, 1.3% KV cache
  - API server alive: /health returns 200, /metrics responds
  - Engine core frozen: Zero tokens generated, forward pass never executes
  - Affects arbitrary request counts: Seen with 11, 124, and other counts
  - Does not self-recover: Requires pod restart
  - --request-timeout does not help: Engine core is frozen, can't enforce timeouts

  Investigation — deadlock tied to CUDA graph code paths:

  Systematic testing to isolate the trigger:
```
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              Config              │               Result               │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Default V1 + async-scheduling    │ DEADLOCK                           │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Default V1 + no async-scheduling │ DEADLOCK                           │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Default V1 + --enforce-eager     │ Didn't run enough but ~8x slower (not viable) │
  └──────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘
```

  Incident 1 (nightly build): During a production spike, autoscaler scaled from 6→20→6 replicas. Two surviving replicas entered deadlock with 123-124 running requests each, stayed frozen 4+ hours until manual restart.

  Incident 2 (v0.17.1 stable): Same deadlock reproduced within minutes of a load test. Single replica, low concurrency (8→16 ramp). Froze at 11 running requests. No autoscaling involved.

  Current workaround: --enforce-eager prevents the deadlock but with ~8x throughput regression, making it unviable for production. Restarting affected replicas is the only practical mitigation.

title: feat(amd): add native GLM MXFP4 Triton Gluon MoE backend
body:
## Motivation GLM-5.2/5.3 decode on MI355X spends a material part of each step in the MoE layer. The existing runner boundary receives already-materialized top-k IDs and weights, so a model-specific kernel cannot optimize across router projection, top-k, route sorting, expert scheduling, activation quantization, routed experts, and the shared expert. This PR adds an **explicit, strict, whole-layer Triton Gluon MoE backend** for the audited GLM Quark MXFP4 contract. Its main optimization is not a standalone faster top-k operation: the selected routes directly become the expert schedule, removing the generic `topk_ids -> moe_sorting -> expert GEMM` handoff. The backend is opt-in and fail-closed. `auto` never selects it, unsupported contracts raise before execution, and a requested Gluon path never silently falls back to AITER or another MoE runner. ## Modifications ### 1. What this adds - `gluon` as a `MoeRunnerBackend` choice. - A reusable whole-layer `GluonMoeBackend` interface with model-specific binding, eager weight preparation, execution, and output ABI validation. - A GLM-5.2/5.3 implementation for serialized Quark W4A4 MXFP4 target experts and the audited BF16 NextN expert layout on gfx950. - Shape-family kernels for decode, speculative verification, and prefill, including continuous TP4/EP1 and TP8/EP1 coverage through a 32K prefill chunk. - TP/EP-aware shared-expert handling and reuse of SGLang's existing post-expert collective/finalization path. Enable the target and speculative paths explicitly: ```bash --moe-runner-backend gluon \ --speculative-moe-runner-backend gluon ``` ### 2. Kernel design The optimized layer owns this model-specific sequence: ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph A["Current SGLang + AITER boundary"] A0["BF16 hidden states"] --> A1["router GEMM"] A1 --> A2["M x 256 logits"] A2 --> A3["biased sigmoid top-8"] A3 --> A4["dense IDs + weights"] A4 --> A5["generic moe_sorting
count, bucket, pad, publish metadata"] A5 --> A6["quantize + GEMM1 + activation + GEMM2"] A6 --> A7["shared expert + add"] end subgraph G["GLM Triton Gluon whole-layer path"] G0["BF16 hidden states"] --> G1["router projection + input quant work
co-scheduled in one launch grid"] G1 --> G2["fixed 256-expert sigmoid top-8"] G2 --> G3{"active-token family"} G3 -->|"tiny M"| G4["selection/expert CTAs share a launch;
expert CTAs recompute the needed route rank"] G3 -->|"medium M"| G5["selection directly emits expert tickets,
sorted routes, and job descriptors"] G3 -->|"large M"| G6["chunk histogram + prefix/scatter
and bucketed grouped projections"] G4 --> G7["MXFP4 experts + shared expert"] G5 --> G7 G6 --> G7 end ``` Important details: - **Tiny M:** the router uses split-K CDNA4 MFMA work to expose enough CTAs on MI355X. Selection is compile-time specialized for 256 experts/top-8. The up-projection launch consumes the selected route directly instead of waiting for a generic sort. - **Medium M:** top-k appends routes directly to expert buckets and publishes the descriptors consumed by the expert projection. - **Large M:** chunked counting, prefix/scatter, and bucketed projections cover prefill shapes. The 32K family splits large routed-partial/code buffers so every gfx950 buffer address remains below the 4-GiB window. - **Quantization:** router projection and activation quantization are independent CTAs in the same launch grid; this removes a host launch and lets both work classes occupy the device together. They are not incorrectly described as a single CTA reading the input once. - **Shared expert:** TP/EP1 target execution consumes SGLang's normal appended shared-expert representation (257 experts). EP and NextN keep the native shared expert and add it before SGLang's existing collective. The isolated measurements below show that standalone top-k is approximately tied with AITER. The useful difference is the producer/consumer boundary: ```text AITER: router -> top-k metadata -> generic MoE sort -> expert work Gluon: router/quant -> top-k becomes the expert schedule -> expert work ``` ### rocprofiler-sdk kernel decomposition To separate GPU work from Python/dispatcher/launch overhead, the full TP8/EP1 MoE call was profiled at PR HEAD `317b7156d` with rocprofiler-sdk 1.1.0 (`--kernel-trace --marker-trace --stats`). Each AITER and Gluon arm was enclosed in its own ROCTx range and repeated 100 times on MI355X. `GPU active` below is the sum of device kernel durations per call. `GPU span` is from the first kernel start to the final kernel end under tracing; its parenthesized component is time between kernels and is profiler-sensitive. The `full MoE` column retains the low-overhead HIP-event result from the table above rather than treating traced wall time as application latency. | M | Path | Kernels / layer | GPU active | Traced GPU span (inter-kernel gaps) | Full MoE, low-overhead | |---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | AITER | 15 | 60.82 us | 649.17 us (587.41 us) | 574.97 us | | 1 | Gluon | 4 | 13.47 us | 70.76 us (57.44 us) | 99.42 us | | 16 | AITER | 14 | 95.57 us | 611.47 us (516.93 us) | 543.89 us | | 16 | Gluon | 3 | 39.05 us | 63.12 us (24.06 us) | 94.34 us | | 32 | AITER | 15 | 119.22 us | 657.49 us (537.73 us) | 706.99 us | | 32 | Gluon | 5 | 64.30 us | 104.74 us (40.52 us) | 159.48 us | The exact AITER device-time decomposition is: | AITER stage | M=1 | M=16 | M=32 | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Router matmul, including BF16-to-FP32 cast where present | 2.69 us | 6.39 us | 7.78 us | | Biased grouped top-k | 4.06 us | 4.96 us | 4.89 us | | Generic route metadata sort/pad | 6.25 us | 9.72 us | 14.06 us | | Routed input quantization + scatter | 2.76 us | 4.25 us | 4.68 us | | Routed gate/up GEMM + SiLU/multiply | 18.11 us | 27.87 us | 36.77 us | | Routed activation quantization + scatter | 2.67 us | 3.02 us | 3.81 us | | Routed down GEMM | 3.82 us | 14.42 us | 19.68 us | | Shared input quantization | 2.15 us | 2.88 us | 3.34 us | | Shared gate/up GEMM, including split-K reduce | 7.90 us | 6.26 us | 7.04 us | | Shared SiLU + multiply | 3.75 us | 8.15 us | 9.15 us | | Shared activation quantization | 1.51 us | 1.96 us | 2.18 us | | Shared down GEMM | 3.43 us | 3.40 us | 3.47 us | | Routed + shared final add | 1.73 us | 2.27 us | 2.37 us | | **Total GPU active** | **60.82 us** | **95.57 us** | **119.22 us** | Gluon performs the same logical work with fused shape-specific stages: | Gluon kernel/stage | M=1 | M=16 | M=32 | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Router GEMM + routed/shared input quantization | 2.48 us | 3.25 us | 3.60 us | | Top-k scheduling + routed/shared gate/up GEMM | 5.18 us | - | - | | Top-k scheduling + routed/shared gate/up + activation quantization | - | 23.91 us | - | | Top-k to expert-job schedule | - | - | 4.61 us | | Routed/shared gate/up GEMM + activation quantization | - | - | 33.80 us | | Activation + quantization | 2.52 us | - | - | | Routed/shared down GEMM + weighted reduction | 3.30 us | 11.89 us | - | | Routed/shared down GEMM | - | - | 18.10 us | | Weighted route reduction + shared add | - | - | 4.19 us | | **Total GPU active** | **13.47 us** | **39.05 us** | **64.30 us** | This changes the interpretation of the earlier isolated timings. At `M=1`, the Gluon `_router_linear` device body is **not** slower: it takes `2.48 us` while also quantizing routed and shared inputs, versus `2.69 us` for AITER's router-only GEMM. The earlier `17-18 us` versus `8-9 us` result measured the complete launch boundary, so it exposed launcher/dispatcher latency rather than slower router arithmetic. The current small-M optimization target should therefore not be the `2.48 us` router body in isolation. ### 3. SGLang integration, isolation, and support matrix The integration sits above `MoeRunnerCore`, because that interface starts after routing has already been computed. The runtime flow is: ```text explicit Gluon selection -> validate quant/model/runtime contract -> bind GLM backend -> prepare packed weights after checkpoint load and before CUDA graph capture -> dispatch by TP/EP, target/NextN, and active M -> validate rank-local output tensor ABI -> existing SGLang _finalize_normal_output / post_experts_all_reduce ``` Isolation from other paths: - `auto` never selects Gluon; AITER, Triton, FlashInfer, MegaMoE, DeepEP, CPU, and other models retain their existing behavior. - GLM modules and Gluon kernels are imported lazily only after explicit selection. - Binding validates `model_type`, hidden/intermediate dimensions, 256 routed experts, sigmoid normalized top-8, quant ABI, gfx950, TP/EP-local shapes, shared-expert state, stream mode, A2A, EPLB, MoE DP, and routed scaling. - Quark layout preparation is owned by the selected backend; Gluon does not construct a dummy AITER runner. - Unsupported M/topology/model/quant combinations raise an actionable error. There is no native/AITER fallback from the Gluon backend. Current audited matrix: | Total TP | EP | Rank-local routed experts | Rank-local intermediate | Target/NextN M coverage | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 4 | 1 | 256 | 512 | 1..32768 | | 4 | 4 | 64 | 2048 | 1..16768 | | 8 | 1 | 256 | 256 | 1..32768 | | 8 | 2 | 128 | 512 | 1..16768 | | 8 | 4 | 64 | 1024 | 1..16768 | | 8 | 8 | 32 | 2048 | 1..16768 | Current model scope: - GLM-5.2/5.3 `glm_moe_dsa` target with serialized Quark W4A4 MXFP4 experts. - GLM NextN/EAGLE draft with the exact audited BF16 expert ABI. This is intentionally not a generic Gluon MoE claim. Future fixed-topology MoEs can reuse the backend boundary, but each model still needs its own strict validator, weight-layout adapter, routing semantics, kernel family, correctness comparison, and performance evidence. The most direct next extension is another GLM-family Quark MXFP4 shape; unrelated models should not be enabled by relaxing the current checks. ## Accuracy Tests ### 4. Kernel correctness - Low-M old/new Gluon schedule comparison at M=1..8: exact bitwise match. - Router/top-k isolation at M=1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128: - identical dense logits: top-8 ID match fraction `1.0`; - maximum top-k weight difference `<= 5.96e-8`; - production split-logit selector vs. dense selector: IDs match `1.0`, weights exactly equal. - EP2/EP4/EP8 compact kernels vs. rank-masked AITER at M=65,96,192,255: - all outputs finite; - relative L2 ranges: `0.004556-0.004568` (EP2), `0.004146-0.004172` (EP4), `0.003849-0.003886` (EP8); - maximum absolute error `<= 9.77e-4`. - Large-M TP8/EP1 Gluon vs. AITER at M=128..32768: relative L2 `1.81%-2.33%`, consistent with different MXFP4 quantization/accumulation order. ### 5. End-to-end correctness Current integration was exercised on GLM-5.2-MXFP4 with EAGLE/NextN, FP8 KV cache, DSA Triton attention, and CUDA graphs: | Topology / arm | Result | |---|---| | TP4/EP4, AITER vs. Gluon | 8/8 exact response texts and 8/8 exact output-token ID sequences | | TP4/EP1, AITER vs. Gluon default shared fusion | 8/8 exact texts and token IDs | | TP4/EP1, AITER vs. Gluon with `--disable-shared-experts-fusion` | 8/8 exact texts and token IDs | Logs confirm the intended shared policy on every rank (EP target/NextN native; EP1 target fused and NextN native) and contain no fallback, skipped Gluon dispatch, assertion, runtime exception, memory access fault, or GPU fault. Strict AgentX functional canaries using the InferenceX workload configuration also completed for TP8/EP2, EP4, and EP8 with target and draft Gluon enabled: 16 backend reports per topology, zero skipped dispatches, zero request/benchmark errors, and no fallback. ### 6. GSM8K **Score: `0.9437` (94.37%, 1,240/1,314 correct).** The full run completed without request errors in 896.44 s at 146.98 output tok/s. This is above the existing 0.92 MI35x GSM8K accuracy threshold used by SGLang's GLM MXFP4 accuracy coverage. Configuration: - full 1,314-question GSM8K test set, 5-shot completion prompt; - GLM-5.2-MXFP4, TP4/EP1, target + NextN Gluon; - EAGLE `3/4/1`, FP8 KV cache, Triton DSA, CUDA graph; - `--chunked-prefill-size 32768`, 256 client threads, temperature 0, maximum 512 output tokens; - strict backend: no fallback. This run also covers the TP4/EP1 large-prefill family. An initial run exposed a real coverage boundary at `M=16802`; the implementation was extended to the full 32K chunk instead of reducing the prefill chunk or hiding the shape behind a fallback. A separate strict request with exactly 32,768 prompt tokens then completed successfully (`prompt_tokens=32768`, one generated token, 8.49 s E2E) with no runtime/GPU error or fallback. ### 7. Test inventory Latest local validation on MI355X: - `72 passed` across: - `test/registered/unit/models/test_gluon_moe_backend.py` - `test/registered/unit/spec/test_draft_construction_isolation.py` - `test/registered/unit/layers/moe/test_fused_shared_expert_scaling.py` - `test/registered/unit/models/test_glm_nextn_moe_ptpc.py` - Continuous dispatch tests enumerate every integer M in each supported range and assert strict rejection immediately outside the audited ranges. - Official Ruff error selection (`F401,F821,F823,UP037`): pass. - Ruff format check over all 25 changed Python files: pass. - `git diff --check`: pass. - Full repository CI: pending; this PR is intentionally opened as Draft. ## Speed Tests and Profiling ### Microbenchmark method - AMD Instinct MI355X, one rank of TP8/EP1 unless stated otherwise. - AITER `acf8fdf9307431ece8ee275971c41cb3d1a7020b`. - PyTorch `2.9.1+rocm7.2.0.git7e1940d4`, Triton `3.8.0`. - 20 warmups, 200 timed repetitions, alternating arm order, HIP-event medians. - The AITER baseline includes SGLang's real small-M sorting patch and native shared-expert work. - Measurements were collected on equivalent pre-rebase kernel revisions; the rebased integration and 32K TP4 adapter were subsequently correctness-tested as described above. #### Route preparation decomposition (microseconds) | M | AITER router + top-k + sort | Gluon router + quant + select/schedule | Speedup | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 62.16 | 32.94 | 1.89x | | 8 | 62.86 | 31.96 | 1.97x | | 16 | 61.48 | 31.90 | 1.93x | | 32 | 200.78 | 47.40 | 4.24x | | 64 | 190.74 | 52.58 | 3.63x | | 128 | 175.76 | 47.06 | 3.73x | At M=1..16, AITER's standalone router is about 2x faster and standalone top-k is approximately tied. The net win comes from eliminating the generic `moe_sorting`/handoff, which costs about 38-50 us by itself. At M>=32, Gluon also has the faster router schedule. #### Complete rank-local MoE layer (microseconds) | M | AITER | Gluon | Speedup | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 574.97 | 99.42 | 5.78x | | 8 | 578.35 | 85.32 | 6.78x | | 16 | 543.89 | 94.34 | 5.77x | | 32 | 706.99 | 159.48 | 4.43x | | 64 | 670.25 | 172.78 | 3.88x | | 128 | 674.65 | 203.26 | 3.32x | A later M=1 fusion removed the standalone activation-quant launch and improved the Gluon arm from `100.80 us / 4 launches` to `81.94 us / 3 launches` (`-18.71%`, exact bitwise output). The shared MTP M=6 schedule improved its isolated layer from `121.44 us / 5 launches` to `85.86 us / 3 launches` (`-29.30%`). #### Large-M complete layer | M | Gluon | AITER | Speedup | Latency reduction | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 128 | 0.153 ms | 0.510 ms | 3.33x | 69.9% | | 1024 | 0.224 ms | 0.563 ms | 2.52x | 60.3% | | 8192 | 0.789 ms | 1.941 ms | 2.46x | 59.4% | | 16384 | 1.370 ms | 3.600 ms | 2.63x | 61.9% | | 32768 | 2.711 ms | 7.042 ms | 2.60x | 61.5% | rocprof confirms that the savings are not only CPU launch timing: | M | AITER launches / GPU-active time | Gluon launches / GPU-active time | |---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 15 / 60.82 us | 4 / 13.47 us (later optimized to 3 launches) | | 16 | 14 / 95.57 us | 3 / 39.05 us | | 32 | 15 / 119.22 us | 5 / 64.30 us | ### AgentX end-to-end performance TP8/EP1, GLM-5.2-MXFP4, MTP `3/4/1`, strict target+draft Gluon, 32K chunk, two-node forward/reverse A/B: Con / MTP | P90 ITV | vs 09/24 baseline | tput/chip | succ request -- | -- | -- | -- | -- C1 3/4/1 | 316.970 | +22.98% | 2338.423 | 258 C1 5/6/1 | 295.403 | +14.62% | 2304.512 | 256 C2 3/4/1 | 243.293 | +29.63% | 2555.224 | 434 C2 5/6/1 | 175.893 | -6.28% | 2419.022 | 409 ## Checklist - [x] Format changed code with Ruff and run the repository's official Ruff error selection. - [x] Add focused unit tests for backend selection, model/quant/topology contracts, shared experts, weight preparation, dispatch coverage, and strict rejection. - [x] Document the design, integration boundary, supported matrix, accuracy, and performance in this PR description. - [x] Provide kernel microbenchmarks, rocprof decomposition, end-to-end performance, and accuracy results. - [x] Follow the SGLang code-style guidance for the changed Python files. - [ ] Run full upstream CI and resolve reviewer feedback. - [ ] Re-run the MTP 5/6/1 C=1 end-to-end arm before marking ready for review. --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :x: [Run #39308947458](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/39308947458) Latest PR Test (Extra): :white_check_mark: [Run #39308947504](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/39308947504) Latest PR Test (AMD ROCm 10): :x: [Run #39308947415](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/39308947415)

title: [Doc] cookbook: Refresh SemiAnalysis AgentX launches with five open InferenceX PRs
body:
[by Claude Code]

## Motivation

The cookbook's **Agentic Long-Context Deployment** sections (#42726, #43083, #43799, #43983, #44065, #44228, #44654, #44712, #45039, #45111) mirror SemiAnalysis InferenceX AgentX submissions as raw launch commands, each linked to the run that measured it. The configurations are mirrored from SemiAnalysis submissions. This PR refreshes all six pages:

1. **Five open InferenceX PRs are overlaid** (table below). New in this round: a Qwen3.5 NVFP4 GB300 Dynamo+SGLang refresh and a DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash H200 SGLang update.
2. **The pages sync to InferenceX `main`** (`660b5a8d`). Several lanes that #45111 showed as in progress have merged and are now verified from the dashboard. Muse Spark Open GB300 enables HiCache above c6.
3. **Lanes no longer overlaid leave or revert.** The knob-tuned GLM-5.2 FP8 B300 lane ([InferenceX #3933](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/3933)) leaves the page. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next B200 and B300 ([InferenceX #4279](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4279) / [#4280](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4280), still WIP) go back to their measured `main` runs. Muse Spark Open H100 is left out this round (below).

## Source

[InferenceX](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX) `main` (`660b5a8d`), with these open InferenceX PRs overlaid:

| PR | Page | Lanes | Pinned to |
|---|---|---|---|
| [#4333](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4333) Qwen3.5 NVFP4 GB300 Dynamo+SGLang | Qwen3.5 | `qwen3.5-fp4-gb300-dynamo-sglang-agentic-agg`, `-disagg`; retires `-agg-pareto`, `-pp-pareto` | no `/use` yet: in progress at head `02b72dc0` |
| [#4327](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4327) DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash H200 SGLang | DeepSeek-V4.1 | `dsv41flash-fp4-h200-sglang-agentic-dspark` | [run 39318221321](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/39318221321), named by the PR's [`/use` comment](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4327#issuecomment-6281433847) (head `5bfd5559`), verified |
| [#4300](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4300) GLM-5.2 NVFP4 GB300 Dynamo+SGLang | GLM-5.2 | `glm5.2-fp4-gb300-dynamo-sglang-agentic-agg`, `-disagg` | in progress at head `8f965ad4` (as in #45111); its [`/use 39187209967`](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4300#issuecomment-6281844799) came after this round's freeze and measured that same commit, so the commands are the measured ones |
| [#4334](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4334) Muse Spark Open B200 SGLang | Muse Spark Open | `musespark-fp4-b200-sglang-agentic-dflash` | no `/use` yet: in progress at head `6a8c8179` |
| [#3817](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/3817) DeepSeek-V4 NVFP4 B300 Dynamo+SGLang (NIXL) | DeepSeek-V4 | `dsv4-fp4-b300-dynamo-sglang-agentic-agg`, `-disagg` | [run 37715955859](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/37715955859), named by the PR's [`/use` comment](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/3817#issuecomment-6072539092) (at `b8bafb34`), verified (as in #45111) |

"In progress" lanes are rendered at the PR head and labeled "In progress in SA InferenceX AgentX". A later sync pins them once the PR gets a `/use` run or merges.

- **[InferenceX #4334](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4334)** takes over from [InferenceX #4221](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4221), which #45111 overlaid. Its diff is identical apart from the changelog's PR link. Since #45111, the head of both PRs moved the B200 image from `dev-muse-spark-open@sha256:8cfc5a72…` to `nightly-dev-20261019-3c560089`. The commands themselves do not change.
- **[InferenceX #4333](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4333)** supersedes [InferenceX #4162](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4162), which #45111 overlaid and which is now closed. It deletes `qwen3.5-fp4-gb300-dynamo-sglang-agentic-agg-pareto` and `-pp-pareto`, so those leave the page as they would when it merges.
- **[InferenceX #3817](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/3817).** Its head has moved past the `/use` run, and that revision has not run yet. The page shows what the run measured.

| [InferenceX #4209](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4209) | `qwen3.5-fp8-h200-sglang-agentic-hicache-mtp` | [run 38965319292](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/38965319292), verified (was in progress; same commands) |

| [InferenceX #4302](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4302) | `musespark-fp4-gb200-sglang-agentic-dflash` | [run 39195111790](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/39195111790), verified (was in progress; same commands) |
| [InferenceX #4317](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4317) | `musespark-fp4-gb300-sglang-agentic-dflash` | [run 39258994981](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/39258994981), verified |
| [InferenceX #4292](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4292) / [#4290](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4290) | `musespark-fp4-b300-sglang-agentic-dflash` / `musespark-fp4-h200-sglang-agentic-dflash` | [run 39181803276](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/39181803276) / [run 39180248743](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/39180248743), verified (full-trace-corpus re-sweeps; same commands) |

- **GLM-5.2 B200 Dynamo+SGLang disagg stays on its measured [InferenceX #3400](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/3400) run.** [InferenceX #4286](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4286) moved the disagg key to the composed recipe format and names it in `perf-changelog.yaml`, but re-swept only the aggregated lane. Its dashboard changelog names only `-agg`, so the disagg lane keeps [run 36304573738](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/36304573738).
- **Qwen3.5 FP8 H200 `-mtp`.** #45111 showed [InferenceX #4209](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4209)'s in-progress revision, which dropped `--tokenizer-path`. #4209's run measured only the HiCache lane, so `-mtp` stays on its last measured run, which passes `--tokenizer-path` (it defaults to the model anyway).
- InferenceX `main` was frozen for this PR at `660b5a8d`. Later merges are left for the next refresh.

## What this PR does

| Page | Lanes | Deployments | Points | Hardware |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GLM-5.2 | 16 (was 17) | 31 (was 34) | 71 (was 78) | GB300, GB200, B300, B200, H200 |

title: StagQ: Constraint-Driven Multi-Precision Weight Quantization for LLMs
body: Serving a large language model (LLM) across a fleet of deployments requires several weight-precision operating points. Multi-precision formats serve them all from one stream whose prefixes are valid lower-precision codes, instead of storing multiple copies. We present StagQ, a multi-precision weight format whose main stream is a 2-bit group-wise affine base followed by a configurable number of 1-bit refinement planes on a dyadic step schedule. Every supported precision is a readable prefix, decoded by an affine map derived from metadata shared across all precisions, with no per-weight lookup. A sparse side record, filled both before and after the grid is fitted, holds out the few weights the grid serves worst. We report two configurations of the encoder. At two bits the cheaper one leads the strongest multi-precision baseline on Llama-3.1-8B, Phi-4, and OLMo-2-7B by 3.1 to 7.0 MMLU points, at a slightly lower logical rate. At three bits it leads on Llama-3.1-8B, leads on Phi-4 at a higher rate, and ties on OLMo-2-7B. At four bits it ties on all three, at a higher rate. In a batch-one matrix-vector product on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, timed on synthetic weights, our kernel is faster than the two baseline kernels in most shape-precision cases.

title: IECZ-III: Hardcore Condensation Lift with Size-Aware Invariants
body: This paper develops a compact, size-aware blueprint for transferring structure through gadget lifts. Two low-order invariants -- cumulative mod-$q$ Fourier mass up to degree $k$ and noise stability $\mathrm{Stab}_ρ$ -- are treated as a reusable "profile" tied to the gadget's affine interface. Under coordinate permutations ($Δ=1$) the profile is preserved exactly; under bounded fan-in the degree budget relaxes by at most $+Δk$ (i.e., $k \mapsto k + Δk$), with all overheads tracked explicitly. In a balanced window $m=(1+γ)n$ the framework yields a distributional lower bound for a monotone cost (Erasure Complexity, EC) and an "echo" to correlation against size-aware $\mathrm{AC}^0{+}\log$ and to logarithmic degree in the polynomial-calculus setting. The accounting keeps total-variation non-expansion and a single $O(\log N)$ prefix-free header visible end to end, avoiding hidden slack.

title: DualMap: Enabling Both Cache Affinity and Load Balancing for Distributed LLM Serving
body: In LLM serving, reusing the KV cache of prompts across requests is critical for reducing TTFT and serving costs. Cache-affinity scheduling, which co-locates requests with the same prompt prefix to maximize KV cache reuse, often conflicts with load-balancing scheduling that distributes requests evenly across compute instances. Existing schedulers fail to reconcile this trade-off as they operate within a single mapping space, typically applying cache-affinity routing to a subset of requests and load-balanced routing to the rest, without a unified solution to achieve both goals. To address this limitation, we propose DualMap, a dual-mapping scheduling strategy for distributed LLM serving that achieves both cache affinity and load balancing. Its key idea is to map each request to two candidate instances via two independent hash functions based on the request prompt, then intelligently select the better candidate based on current system states. This design increases the likelihood that requests with shared prefixes are co-located, while evenly dispersing distinct prefixes across the cluster via ``the power of two choices''. To make DualMap robust under dynamic and skewed real-world workloads, we incorporate three techniques: 1) SLO-aware request routing, which prioritizes cache affinity but switches to load-aware scheduling when TTFT exceeds the SLO, enhancing load balance without sacrificing cache reuse; 2) hotspot-aware rebalancing, which dynamically migrates requests from overloaded to underloaded instances, mitigating hotspots and rebalancing the system; 3) lightweight dual-hash-ring scaling, which leverages a dual-hash-ring mapping to support fast and low-overhead instance scaling without costly global remapping. Experiments on real-world workloads show that DualMap improves effective request capacity by up to 2.25times under the same TTFT SLO constraints compared with SOTA work.

title: SIDScope: A Diagnostic Resource for Semantic-ID Interfaces in Generative Recommendation
body: Semantic-ID mappings are reusable interfaces between item tokenizers and generative recommenders, yet released mappings rarely state whether they are coherent, what structure they expose, how generated paths resolve, or what must be revalidated after a refresh. SIDScope is a source-traced diagnostic resource for these decisions. It normalizes item-to-code artifacts, verifies provenance and joins, profiles mapping structure, compares paired revisions, and accounts for path-to-item outcomes in generated traces. Across nine source-traced tokenizer exports from seven families on Amazon and Yelp data - eight executable routes plus one auditable snapshot - SIDScope reveals that interface health is multi-signal rather than scalar. Its central finding is mechanism-conditional: prefix alignment strongly tracks held-out candidate exposure when retrieval consumes SID prefixes, then weakens as scoring becomes prefix-independent. Trained trace accounting exposes a second hidden gap: a valid target path can survive without uniquely retrieving the target item by 1.2-3.0 percentage points. A refresh case establishes a third: repairing the mapping does not by itself restore an inherited generator; model reuse requires a separate handoff check. The package provides frozen evidence summaries, conformance reports, trace labels, table builders, and CPU-only verifiers. It supports decisions about artifact readiness, interface risks, and revalidation before model reuse.

title: Efficient and Interpretable Multi-Agent LLM Routing via Ant Colony Optimization
body: Large Language Model (LLM)-driven Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) have demonstrated strong capability in complex reasoning and tool use, and heterogeneous agent pools further broaden the quality--cost trade-off space. Despite these advances, real-world deployment is often constrained by high inference cost, latency, and limited transparency, which hinders scalable and efficient routing. Existing routing strategies typically rely on expensive LLM-based selectors or static policies, and offer limited controllability for semantic-aware routing under dynamic loads and mixed intents, often resulting in unstable performance and inefficient resource utilization. To address these limitations, we propose AMRO-S, an efficient and interpretable routing framework for Multi-Agent Systems (MAS). AMRO-S models MAS routing as a semantic-conditioned path selection problem, enhancing routing performance through three key mechanisms: First, it leverages a supervised fine-tuned (SFT) small language model for intent inference, providing a low-overhead semantic interface for each query; second, it decomposes routing memory into task-specific pheromone specialists, reducing cross-task interference and optimizing path selection under mixed workloads; finally, it employs a quality-gated asynchronous update mechanism to decouple inference from learning, optimizing routing without increasing latency. Extensive experiments on five public benchmarks and high-concurrency stress tests demonstrate that AMRO-S consistently improves the quality--cost trade-off over strong routing baselines, while providing traceable routing evidence through structured pheromone patterns.

title: Add B300 Dynamo+SGLang AgentX configs for DeepSeek V4 with NIXL KV transfer / 添加使用 NIXL KV 传输的 DeepSeek V4 B300 Dynamo+SGLang AgentX 配置
body:
[by Claude Code]

## Summary

Adds DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 FP4 B300 Dynamo+SGLang AgentX recipes. The recipes come from #3631, with disaggregated KV transfer over NIXL instead of Mooncake, and now run on `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-efa-20261019-3c560089`.

- **Points:** aggregate TP8 c1, TP4 c4, TP4 c8 (HiCache) and DEP8 c384 (HiCache); disaggregated 1P1D DEP8 c64/c240 and 1P2D DEP8 c64 (HiCache prefill). Topology, concurrency, cache sizes and memory fractions are unchanged.
- **Image:** `nightly-dev-efa-20261019-3c560089`, the AWS EFA variant of the 2026-10-19 nightly (sgl-project/sglang#41006), replaces `nightly-dev-20260916-c9a8fba9`.
  - On `nightly-dev-20261013-7224fce1`, the disaggregated workers failed at NIXL startup with `createBackend: unsupported backend 'LIBFABRIC'`. The LIBFABRIC plugin of NIXL 1.5.0 needs libfabric's `FABRIC_1.7` symbol version, and the regular image ships only Ubuntu's libfabric 1.17, which stops at `FABRIC_1.6`. The cluster no longer injects the host's libfabric into containers, so nothing newer was available.
  - The EFA variant adds AWS EFA installer 1.50.0 (libfabric 2.6.0) and puts `/opt/amazon/efa/lib` first on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`. Its build checks that the NIXL plugin resolves libfabric there.
- **Attention DP:** DEP8 workers set `attn-dp-size: 8` in place of `dp-size: 8` + `enable-dp-attention: true`, which sgl-project/sglang#41818 deprecated.
- **Dynamo:** the recipes use the image's bundled Dynamo `1.6.0.dev20261018` (`dynamo.install: false`), which is also the router version in the master config.
  - It includes ai-dynamo/dynamo#16005, which counts attention-DP ranks from `attn_dp_size`. In this SGLang, both DP spellings resolve to `dp_size=1, attn_dp_size=8`. A Dynamo without that fix registers one DP rank per DEP8 worker and subscribes only to rank 0's KV events, so the KV router sends every request to DP rank 0.
  - The previous revision built Dynamo `b208989fbe` from source, because the 1013 image's bundled `1.6.0.dev20261010` predated that fix.
- **Disaggregated KV transfer:** NIXL with the LIBFABRIC backend (`SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_NIXL_BACKEND=LIBFABRIC`, which the EFA image also sets by default). The image's NIXL 1.5.0 ships the plugin and the image ships the libfabric it needs, so there is no setup script, waiver or package change.
  - Both disaggregated workers set `FI_EFA_USE_UNSOLICITED_WRITE_RECV=0`. NIXL's LIBFABRIC backend disables the EFA provider's unsolicited write recv only when built against libfabric 2.3 or newer. The image's NIXL is not (its "Successfully disabled unsolicited write recv" log line never appears), so with the image's libfabric 2.6 the feature stays on.
  - With it on, the previous sweep of this PR (run 39191181928, two attempts of 1P1D c240) had about 1.4% of requests time out on decode after 900 s. Prefill had already sent their KV, but the completions never reached decode. Throughput per GPU fell from about 60k (0916 image) to 44k tok/s.
- **Image behavior to note:**
  - This SGLang fuses the shared expert into the DeepGEMM Mega-MoE kernel by default (sgl-project/sglang#39313), so DEP8 throughput may differ from earlier runs of these recipes for that reason too.
  - The EFA image sets `NCCL_NET_PLUGIN=ofi` and `NCCL_TUNER_PLUGIN=ofi` (aws-ofi-nccl 1.21.1) by default. Every worker in these recipes fits on one node.
- No recipe enables the W4A4 MXFP4 Mega-MoE path. Prefill and decode use the same DSpark K=6 method.
- On `b300-dsxe`, Dynamo+SGLang serves DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 from the node-local NVMe copy (`DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813@scratch`), as vLLM already does.
- **Aggregate DEP8 c384 scheduling:** adopts the scheduling settings of the single-node SGLang EAGLE DEP8 recipe (`dsv4-fp4-b300-sglang-agentic-hicache-eagle`): `enable-mixed-chunk: true`, `schedule-policy: shortest-prefill-first`, `SGLANG_ENABLE_DP_SPEC_PREFILL_COORDINATION=1` and `prefill-decode-interval: 32` (was 20).
  - In run 39191181928 this point queued prefills behind decode: TTFT p50 33.5 s and p90 89 s, against 2.9 s and 12.7 s for the EAGLE standalone c384 point.
  - The gap came from these settings, not from Dynamo routing. About 96% of requests followed session affinity, and uncached prefill per DP rank was within ±3%. The DSpark standalone recipe this point was ported from has the same gap.
  - With mixed chunk, a step carries at most 8192 prefill tokens plus 96 one-token decodes per rank, within the existing `SGLANG_OPT_DEEPGEMM_MEGA_MOE_NUM_MAX_TOKENS_PER_RANK=8320`.
- **Recipe format:** the master config selects the recipes with `srt-recipe-dir` and `srt-recipe` (#3805), and the recipes are fragments without the keys the launcher binds (#3818), as on current `main`.

<details>
<summary>Settings removed or renamed since the 0916 image</summary>

Checked against the SGLang source at `7224fce1` and the Dynamo source at `b208989fbe`, then rechecked for the current image. Between SGLang `7224fce1` and `3c560089`, no arg or env var these recipes use was renamed, removed or given a new default. Between Dynamo `b208989fbe` and the bundled `1.6.0.dev20261018`, the Dynamo flags and env vars the recipes set, and the defaults cited below, are unchanged. Topology declarations (`tp-size`, `ep-size`, and `dp-size: 1` on TP points) are kept.

| Setting | Roles | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `SGLANG_OPT_SWA_SPLIT_LEAF_ON_INSERT`, `SGLANG_OPT_USE_JIT_NORM`, `SGLANG_OPT_USE_DEEPGEMM_MEGA_MOE`, `SGLANG_DSV4_MHC_PREWARM` | various | The image no longer reads them. `moe-a2a-backend: megamoe` selects Mega-MoE, and MHC prewarm always runs. |
| `SGLANG_OPT_DEEPGEMM_MEGA_MOE`, `NCCL_TIMEOUT` | disagg | Never defined: the first is a misspelling, and the second is not an NCCL variable. |
| `SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING`, `SGLANG_DSV4_REASONING_EFFORT`, `SGLANG_REQUEST_STATE_WAIT_TIMEOUT` | all, disagg | Only SGLang's own HTTP server reads them. Behind Dynamo, the frontend applies the chat template with thinking and reasoning effort taken from the request, and the worker calls the engine directly. |

<details>
<summary>Recipe details (carried over from #3631)</summary>

### Aggregate DEP8 c384

Ported from the single-node SGLang DEP8 c384 point (`dsv4-fp4-b300-sglang-agentic-hicache-mtp`, `benchmarks/single_node/srt-slurm-recipes/dsv4/sglang/b300-fp4-mtp/agentic.yaml`, `override_dep8_c384`):

- **Engine settings kept:** DP8 attention + EP8 Mega-MoE, FP4 indexer, DP LM head, local control broadcast, prefill delayer (interval now 32, see above), `stream-interval: 20`, `chunked-prefill-size: 65536` with `SGLANG_OPT_DEEPGEMM_MEGA_MOE_NUM_MAX_TOKENS_PER_RANK=8320`, `max-running-requests: 768` (96 per DP rank, twice concurrency), `mem-fraction-static: 0.88`, `swa-full-tokens-ratio: 0.075`, HiCache ratio 3 (`write_back`, `direct`, `page_first_direct`), DSpark K=6.
- **Decode graph limit:** `cuda-graph-max-bs-decode: 96`, the per-rank request cap (768 / 8).
- **Routing:** the Dynamo KV router replaces the SGLang router's DP-aware consistent hashing. Sessions stay sticky through `X-Dynamo-Session-ID`, and each DP rank publishes KV events (`kv-events-config`). The frontend sets `DYN_TCP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT: "60"`, as the disaggregated recipes do, so the c384 warmup burst does not exceed Dynamo's 5 s request-plane ack timeout.
- **Dropped:** settings that only apply to SGLang's own HTTP server and have no effect behind the Dynamo frontend: `tokenizer-worker-num`, tool-call and reasoning parsers, chat template, `skip-server-warmup`, `SGLANG_TIMEOUT_KEEP_ALIVE`.

### Gap-filling points: agg TP4 c8 and disagg 1P2D DEP8 c64

- **Agg TP4 c8:** the TP4 c4 recipe with `max-running-requests: 16` and `cuda-graph-max-bs-decode: 16`, plus a HiCache DRAM tier (`hicache-ratio: 2.75`, `write_through`, `direct`, `page_first_direct`), because TP4 c4 already fills about 60% of the GPU KV pool.
- **Disagg 1P2D DEP8 c64:** the 1P1D c64 recipe with a second decode worker (3 nodes), which halves each decode rank's load.

### NIXL instead of Mooncake

On AWS EFA, Mooncake needs the separate `mooncake-transfer-engine-efa-cuda13` wheel in place of the image's Mooncake package, which #3631 installed during container setup ([review](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/3631#discussion_r4201491559)). NIXL ships its own LIBFABRIC plugin, and the EFA image provides the libfabric it needs, so these recipes drop that setup script, its waiver and the Mooncake-only settings (`MOONCAKE_PROTOCOL`, `MC_MS_FILTERS`, `WITH_NVIDIA_PEERMEM`). The NIXL LIBFABRIC settings come from #3597.

</details>

body:
Rewrite of #4336 with three differences. First, the disaggregated DEP2 prefill workers back their Engram host tables with per-rank transparent huge pages (`use_thp: true`, `dp_shared_memory: false`) instead of the DP-shared pinned tables. Second, the disaggregated curve runs only 10P1D DEP2/DEP16 at concurrency 7888 (was 8400), dropping the 9P1D c7480 point. Third, no GB300 nodes are excluded. title: perf(dsv4): route DP-attention agentic traffic with cache_aware / 用 cache_aware 路由 DP-attention 智能体流量
body:
> **Draft.** The root-cause analysis below is measured. The specific fix
> (`cache_aware`) is not yet validated end-to-end; I am running that now and
> will post numbers before marking this ready.

## Why

`dsv4 fp4 mi355x vllm TP8/DPA mtp c128` reaches a **90.5%** GPU prefix cache hit
rate against a **95.5%** theoretical ceiling, while the matching ATOM point
reaches **92.4%** against **95.9%**.

- vLLM: [run 34774626435 / job 103780081837](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/34774626435/job/103780081837)
- ATOM: [run 33376779864 / job 99523226161](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/33376779864/job/99523226161)

Normalising against each run's own ceiling, ATOM converts 96.4% of the
theoretically cacheable tokens into hits and vLLM only 94.7%.

## Root cause

Under `--data-parallel-size 8` each DP rank is a separate engine with its own KV
pool (`GPU KV cache size: 6,259,837 tokens` x8) and its own prefix cache. A
request only hits if it lands on the rank that already holds its prefix.

The launcher pins sessions with `--policy consistent_hash` plus
`AIPERF_HTTP_X_SESSION_ID_FROM_CORRELATION_ID=1`. That works exactly as written
— `router.log` shows session keys spread evenly over the 8 ranks (10.4%–15.9%
of sessions each). The problem is the choice of key.

Joining the run's `profile_export.jsonl` against `router.log`:

| | |
|---|---|
| trajectories (`root_correlation_id` / `source_trace_id`) | 216 |
| distinct `x_correlation_id` values used as routing keys | 1,440 |
| requests at `agent_depth` 1 (sub-agent branches) | 4,707 / 7,569 |
| trajectories scattered over 2–8 DP ranks | **99 / 216 (45.8%)** |
| trajectories scattered over all 8 ranks | 13 (6.0%) |
| prompt tokens belonging to a split trajectory | **446M / 819M (54.5%)** |

The agentic trace fans one trajectory out into several sub-agent branches that
inherit the parent's context. Each branch gets its own correlation ID, so
`consistent_hash` sends it to a different rank, and that rank has to prefill the
shared prefix into its own pool again.

Per-rank hit rates track this: 87.1% / 87.5% / 89.4% / 90.3% / 90.4% / 91.6% /
91.9% / 92.3% (volume-weighted 90.48%, matching the reported 90.5%).

## Evidence for the mechanism

On an 8xMI355X box I brought up the same config locally (same args, same
`block size 256` / `DEEPSEEK_SPARSE_SWA`, 6,336,403 tokens per rank) and replayed
a synthetic workload shaped like the trace — one long shared trajectory prefix,
seven sub-agent branches — pinning each request with `X-data-parallel-rank` so
routing was the only variable:

| routing key | prefix cache hit rate | wall | mean TTFT |
|---|---|---|---|
| per-branch (what we do today) | 9.19% | 768s | 83.0s |
| per-trajectory | **64.90%** | 406s | 43.0s |
| single shared cache | 64.90% | 956s | 105.0s |

Co-locating a trajectory's branches recovers everything a single shared cache
would give for this shape, which says the partitioning itself is fine and the
routing key is what hurts.

Please read those absolute numbers as a mechanism check, not a prediction of the
production delta: the synthetic deliberately contains no within-branch multi-turn
reuse, which is where most real hits come from and which already works today.

## The change

`cache_aware` is vllm-router's own default. It keeps a radix tree of prompt
prefixes, routes to the rank holding the longest match, and falls back to load
balancing once a rank is `--balance-abs-threshold` (64) requests ahead. It keys
on prompt content, so it co-locates sub-agent branches without any session
header, and it also captures prefixes shared *across* trajectories (system
prompt, tool definitions, common repo context) that no session-keyed policy can
catch. `AIPERF_HTTP_X_SESSION_ID_FROM_CORRELATION_ID` becomes unused and is
dropped.

## Open questions for review

1. **Validation.** I have not yet run the full `aiperf` replay under
   `cache_aware`. Doing that here needs `semianalysisai/cc-traces-weka-062126`,
   which is not in the local HF cache. Happy to drive it through CI instead if
   that is easier.
2. **Load balance.** `cache_aware` trades balance for locality. With ISL p95 at
   373k tokens and only 5.97x max concurrency per rank, the default
   `cache_threshold 0.3` / `balance_abs_threshold 64` may need tuning. Worth a
   sweep?
3. **Scope.** `dsv4_fp4_b200_vllm_mtp.sh` and `dsv4_fp4_b300_vllm_mtp.sh` carry
   the identical `consistent_hash` block. I left them alone until this is
   validated on MI355X — say the word and I will include them.

## Unrelated finding, not fixed here

`VLLM_PREFIX_CACHE_RETENTION_INTERVAL=32768` (set just below this block) is a
no-op. The CI log shows `Unknown vLLM environment variable detected:
VLLM_PREFIX_CACHE_RETENTION_INTERVAL`, and the run's own
`vllm:cache_config_info` reports `prefix_cache_retention_interval 0`. The name
also does not exist in current vLLM nightly (`0.3.1.dev251+g0961bbae2`). Since
the comment cites vllm-project/vllm#43447 and #44774 for SWA prefix-cache
retention, someone who knows the intent should decide whether to drop it or
chase the real knob. Left untouched to keep this diff to one concern.

title: [NVIDIA][AgentX] GB300 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Dynamo+SGLang: DEP2/DEP16 disaggregated points on the 20261020 nightly with the Mooncake linker / [NVIDIA][AgentX] GB300 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Dynamo+SGLang：基于 20261020 nightly 与 Mooncake linker 的 DEP2/DEP16 分离式配置点
body:
Follows #4180 (merged) and moves the GB300 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Dynamo + SGLang disaggregated points to `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20261020-ab580b2e` (multiarch digest pinned) with the ai-dynamo `1.6.0.dev20261019` it ships. The disaggregated points switch from prefill HiCache to the Mooncake external cache linker on both roles, and use the `flashmla_mega` attention backend. c1228 now runs 3 DEP2 prefill workers instead of 4 and c2884 5 instead of 6, and a c4096 point is added. A setup script applies the one SGLang change the image does not contain yet (#44623). The aggregated points from #4180 are unchanged.

| Config key | Topology | Conc | Nodes (GPUs) | Key settings |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `dsv41flash-fp4-gb300-dynamo-sglang-agentic-dspark-disagg` | 3x DEP2 prefill + 1x DEP16 decode | 1228 | 7 (22) | Mooncake store segment 80gb prefill / 140gb decode, 24 requests per decode rank, 36 extra decode slots |
| | 5x DEP2 prefill + 1x DEP16 decode | 2884 | 8 (26) | segment 80gb prefill / 140gb decode, 40 requests per decode rank, 80 extra decode slots, prefill batches capped at 32768 tokens |
| | 7x DEP2 prefill + 1x DEP16 decode | 4096 | 9 (30) | segment 80gb prefill / 140gb decode, 64 requests per decode rank, 128 extra decode slots, prefill batches capped at 32768 tokens |

An odd number of DEP2 workers leaves two GPUs of the last prefill node idle (c1228: 2 prefill nodes, c2884: 3, c4096: 4). The master rows count only the GPUs in use: 6, 10 and 14 prefill + 16 decode = 22, 26 and 30 GPUs. Like #4180, both points use a dedicated CPU node for the frontend and the AgentX client.

Shared disaggregated settings:

- MegaMoE all-to-all, `dsv4-attn-backend: flashmla_mega`, DSpark block size 5, Mooncake KV transfer, local DP control broadcast (`enable-dp-attention-local-control-broadcast`), host Engram tables, 2048 SWA prefix tails and decoder SWA bounded replay on both roles.
- Mooncake external cache linker on both roles (`enable-unified-cache-external-linker`, Mooncake backend, group semantics), with a `mooncake-master` service (`--eviction_high_watermark_ratio=0.90 --client_ttl=60 --rpc_thread_num=64`). The linker and `enable-hierarchical-cache` are mutually exclusive in SGLang, so the master rows now declare `kv-offload-backend: mooncake 0.3.13.post1`.
- Prefill: mega mHC (`SGLANG_OPT_DSV41_MEGA_MHC_PREFILL=1`), MegaMoE cap of 32768 tokens per rank, chunked prefill of 65536.
- Decode: stream interval 32, polling interval 8, MegaMoE cap of 16384 tokens per rank, 8 gateway workers, metrics off.
- Drops `SGLANG_NCCL_ALL_GATHER_IN_OVERLAP_SCHEDULER_SYNC_BATCH`: the image already exchanges the scheduler's MLP sync rows with a gloo gather + broadcast (sgl-project/sglang#44622).
- Dynamo uses the ZMQ event plane with the TCP request plane, so the NATS service is dropped. The frontend is NUMA-bound.

SGLang patches (`configs/dsv41flash-sglang-patches.sh` applies `configs/dsv41flash-sglang-patches/*.patch` to `/sgl-workspace/sglang`, which is the image's editable install; it uses `git apply`, is idempotent, holds a lock across workers on the same node, and fails the worker if any hunk does not apply):

| Patch | Upstream | Fixes |
|---|---|---|
| `sglang-pr44623.patch` | sgl-project/sglang#44623 (open) | Lets the external cache linker register DeepSeek-V4.1's hybrid KV pools (pool assemblers, unified linker, Mooncake/UMBP direct linkers) |

Drop the patch once the pinned image contains it. The 20261020 image already contains sgl-project/sglang#44580 and #45062, which earlier revisions of this PR carried as patches.

### Local validation

One or two 3600 s AgentX runs per point on GB300 NVL72 with the CI benchmark script and launch environment, golden acceptance 3.51, 0 failed requests. Throughput counts input tokens per GPU in use (22, 26 and 30).

| Point | Image and SGLang changes | tok/s/GPU | P90 TTFT (p50) | P90 / median tok/s/user |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1228, 3P1D | 20261016 image + #44623, #44580 and the prefill fixes the 20261019 image later shipped | 364.5k / 362.1k (2 runs) | 2.6 s (0.9 s) | 235-237 / 251-252 |
| c2884, 5P1D | 20261019 image + #44623, #44580, #45062 (this PR's previous head) | 604.4k | 10.3 s (4.4 s) | 178 / 191 |
| c4096, 7P1D | same as c2884 | 630.1k | 15.0 s (8.7 s) | 137 / 145 |

#44580 and #45062 are in the 20261020 image, so these stacks match this PR apart from the nightly date. The c1228 and c4096 runs also carried a decode admission-ordering patch that this PR does not include; it measured no difference (P90 230/232 without vs 230/228 with, two same-time pairs at c1228). The 20261020 image itself has not been run yet.

<summary>中文</summary>

title: github:deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM:350 fetched implementation patch
Add SM90 BF16 grouped GEMM with gathered activation rows
body:
Routed BF16 forward paths currently materialize `a.index_select(0, rows)` before grouped GEMM. This adds `m_grouped_bf16_gemm_nt_contiguous_gathered(a, b, d, grouped_layout, a_row_indices)` on SM90, loading A through row indices directly into the existing WGMMA pipeline.

The first version supports K-major BF16, K divisible by 64, contiguous weights, 128-row expert alignment and an int64 CUDA row map. A may have a padded row stride. The A loader uses 16-byte `cp.async` copies with the existing shared-memory swizzle; B/output retain TMA. It does not add a fused SwiGLU epilogue or change default dispatch.

## Current revision

Commit `ca1291f7cd2dbe483af7d89f033b2a5a1e96ca1f`, based on main `1fc9c66975ee322d628b3288534ca0e9ce12a64d`, keeps the change in six existing files:

- Public API and registration in `csrc/apis/gemm.hpp`; configuration, TMA descriptors and launch in the existing SM90 implementation header.
- Integrated coverage in `tests/test_bf16.py`, rather than a separate gathered test file. It covers three generated configurations, six boundary cases and three rejected invalid inputs.
- The CUDA kernel's executable tokens are unchanged from the previous published revision. Host checks are reorganized while retaining the dimensionality, dtype, device, row-stride, alignment and empty-input constraints.

The native extension was forcibly rebuilt from this exact source and the focused gathered test passed on the original H200/SM90 stack: PyTorch `2.13.0+cu132`, CUDA runtime 13.2, seed 42, strict deterministic algorithms and uninitialized-memory filling disabled. All generated results are checked bitwise against the materialized path. Both paths use CUDA events in the integrated test, but those printed timings are not a new controlled performance result.

This is build/numerical/boundary validation, not a rerun of the historical full integration, sanitizer or performance studies below.

## Earlier 2.8.1 measurements

The following results were collected against the 2.8.1 release, #462 (`057ca5964aae0879ff2e0eb71ee05a3cb0ba3df7`), at PR commit `0ff99780929827f24f19d5e67a10c390c5f77592`.

On eight H200s, against activation gather + the existing GEMM with **prepacked gate/up weights** + the same fused output-compaction/SwiGLU kernel:

| D=3072, F=1280, 16 experts | Eager reduction, run 1 / repeat | CUDA Graph reduction |
|---|---:|---:|
| R=8192, M=16384, random routes | 6.42% / 6.31% | — |
| R=108031, M=170003, random routes | 6.07% / 5.83% | — |
| Source-ordered routes, nominal shape | 6.18% | 5.78% |
| Source-ordered routes, packet stride D+64 | 6.39% | 6.16% |

Eager numbers are median per-GPU ABBA/BAAB reductions; Graph is one GPU. The general eager sweep uses random routes with replacement, while Graph uses source-ordered unique routes; only the explicitly source-ordered rows compare matching routes across modes. Workers and process repeats reuse seed 42. An additional same-GPU, matching-row-map test at R=8192/M=16384 measures 6.25% eager / 6.01% Graph. The small R=1024, M=512, D=F=256 case measures 26.07% eager but **regresses 2.31% under Graph**, on matching routes. This is a fixed-route forward benchmark, not a full-model speedup.

All tested h/gate/up outputs match both existing-library baselines bitwise. API tests cover partial/empty M, empty experts, source/output stride, aligned offsets and misaligned pointer rejection. An additional 79-case regression covers existing BF16 GEMM/einsum layouts, output dtypes and accumulation modes using exact references and bytewise repeats. Independent FP32 reference checks pass; compute-sanitizer memcheck reports 0 errors. The full 13-phase 2.8.1 run passed, including live EP8 integration and receive-view lifetime checks; combined forward reductions are 16.99%–17.59% across two runs when both this change and [DeepEP #769](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP/pull/769) are enabled.

[2.8.1 reproducer, raw cycles, source hashes and limitations](https://gist.github.com/yuweih205/d3fd1e4c3fcb97364f36ec8fda996cfe#file-dg281-infra-report-md). These measurements retain their original test revision and predate the current reorganization; this update makes no additional performance claim. The earlier 2.8.0 measurements remain separately preserved in the same Gist.

Before this reorganization, the PR test scripts also passed a separate eight-H200 correctness rerun against the frozen production-equivalent runtimes. That DeepEP test revision checked an independent input/route oracle, raw deterministic order and two delayed consumer streams under both record-stream policies. [Exact test revisions and retained test-development failures](https://gist.github.com/yuweih205/d3fd1e4c3fcb97364f36ec8fda996cfe#file-review-gates-report-md).

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash stores each KV token as 528B: 512B of FP8 E4M3 covering
the full 512-wide K (rope lanes quantized, no BF16 rope segment) plus a 16B

deepseek-ai/FlashMLA#221

groundwork: GLM53_NOPE-style geometry (D_ROPE=0) composed with a 32-wide
UE8M0 footer.

Kernel side the format is simpler than DSV4 (one 512B bulk per row, a single
unified block-scaled FP8 QK pass, no rope MMA paths). The two new mechanics:

- the 16B footer row generalizes the scale gather from one uint64_t to a
